chapterBreakdown.gentle: You probably already know what it feels like when a conversation slides without anyone choosing to slide it. One minute someone is making a calm point about a code change. The next minute they sound like a tired teacher, and you find yourself sitting up a little straighter, the way you used to in middle school. Eric Berne built a small tool for noticing this. He said an adult, at any moment, is speaking from one of three places inside themselves. There is the Parent voice, made of rules and shoulds picked up early. There is the Adult voice, which looks at what is in front of it and handles information in the present. And there is the Child voice, which still carries the original feelings of being little. Nobody is only one of these. The point is to start hearing which voice is in the room right now.
chapterBreakdown.direct: At any moment, an adult is operating from one of three observable states. Berne called them Parent, Adult, and Child. Parent is the voice of the rules a person learned from early authority figures. Adult is the voice that handles current information neutrally and can update on new evidence. Child is the voice that still carries the original feelings from one's own childhood. These are not personality types. They are states a single person moves through, sometimes several times in a single conversation. The signals are external: voice, posture, vocabulary, the kind of reply the speaker is unconsciously demanding. When a code review comment shifts mid-sentence from technical note to scolding, the speaker has just moved from Adult to Parent. When a graduate student answers a professor from a hurt place instead of a thinking one, that is Adult sliding into Child. The model is for noticing those moves.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: In any conversation that matters, you are not just exchanging information with one person. You are exchanging it with whichever of their three voices is currently in the room, and you are answering from one of your three. Miss the shift and you will spend the next ten minutes losing an argument you did not know you were in. Berne's three states give you a faster read. The Parent voice runs on rules. The Adult voice runs on present-tense facts. The Child voice runs on old feelings still alive in a grown body. Watch a colleague's tone drop a register mid-sentence and you have just watched a state change. Most of the cost in a stalled meeting, a tense one-on-one, or a kitchen argument is paid because nobody noticed which voice arrived. Reading the voice in the room first is the cheapest leverage you have.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Most people, when they think about how a conversation works, picture two minds exchanging sentences. Eric Berne thought that was too simple. He noticed that the same person could speak in two completely different voices inside the same five minutes, and that the people they were speaking to would respond to the change before they could even name it. So he built a small vocabulary, deliberately plain, that anyone could use without therapy training.

His claim was that at any moment an adult is in one of three states. Not three personality types. Three voices a single person moves through. Parent is the voice of the rules and judgments and shoulds that a person picked up from the authority figures of their early life. It comes in two flavors: a critical version that finds fault and corrects, and a nurturing version that takes care and reassures. Both are still Parent. A warm voice telling you what you should feel is not less Parent for being warm. Adult is the voice that observes what is in front of it, in the present, and handles information without coloring it. It is the only state that can update its mind on new evidence. Child is the voice that still carries the original emotional life of one's own childhood, the wanting, the curiosity, the hurt, the rebellious flicker, the wish to be approved of. None of these states is a problem on its own. A person without access to their Child is not healthier; they are flatter.

What makes the model useful is not the names. It is that the signals are external. You can see a state change from the outside. When Priya's code-review comment shifted from technical to scolding in its last clause, what changed was not her information about Marcus's code. What changed was her register, and Marcus's shoulders answered the change before his fingers did. That is the level the model is built to operate on. Not the inside of a person's head, but the visible texture of how they are talking right now. The work, on a first reading, is just to start hearing it.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne's first claim is that adult behavior is not one thing. The same person, in the same room, in a single conversation, can switch between several distinct ways of speaking, thinking, and reacting. He called these ways ego states, and he proposed that there are three of them in active use at any moment: Parent, Adult, and Child.

Parent is the residue of the authority figures of the person's early life. It speaks in rules ('this is how it is done'), judgments ('that was lazy work'), shoulds and shouldn'ts. It has a Critical face, which restricts and finds fault, and a Nurturing face, which protects and reassures. Both are Parent. Adult is the present-tense state. It evaluates current information and decides based on the situation actually in front of it. It is neutral in tone. It is the only state that can revise its position on new evidence. Child is what remains, in the grown person, of the emotional and reactive patterns of their own childhood. It contains creativity, curiosity, original feeling, and old strategies for handling authority figures.

The reason this scheme is useful is the source of its evidence. The states are observable. They show up as changes in voice register, vocabulary choice, posture, and the kind of reply the speaker is unconsciously demanding. When a senior engineer's code-review comment shifts mid-sentence into a teacher's tone, the comment's information has not changed but the engineer's state has, and the junior engineer reading the comment can feel the shift before they can name it. When a graduate student's factual question is answered by a professor as if it were a challenge, the question came from Adult and the answer came from Parent, and the room can feel the mismatch immediately even though no one has the vocabulary for it. The model gives that vocabulary. The first job of a reader using it is not to fix anything. It is to start hearing which voice is currently in the room and which voice is answering it.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Three quarters of the conversations that go badly do not go badly because the people involved are stupid or hostile. They go badly because both people quietly changed who was talking partway through and neither of them noticed. Berne built a tool for catching that.

The tool is a small, deliberately blunt vocabulary. At any moment, an adult is operating from one of three states: Parent, Adult, or Child. Parent is the voice of the rules a person absorbed from early authority. It speaks in shoulds and judgments, and it has both a critical edge and a nurturing edge, but a nurturing voice telling you what you should feel is still Parent, and is still doing work the speaker cannot quite see. Adult is the voice that handles what is actually in front of it, in present tense, and is the only state that can take in new evidence without distorting it. Child is the original emotional life of the person, still resident in a grown body: the wanting, the hurt, the cleverness, the small flare of rebellion. These are not three kinds of people. They are three voices any one person carries, and they trade off without asking permission.

The leverage in the model is that the signals are external. State shifts show up in voice, posture, word choice, and the kind of reply the speaker is unconsciously trying to pull from the room. A code-review comment that begins as a technical note and ends as a tired teacher's correction has changed states mid-sentence. A graduate student's hand goes up to ask a factual question, and a professor answers as if his authority has been challenged: the question came from Adult, the answer came from Parent, and the discussion is now in a smaller room than it was a minute ago. People who can read those moves at the level of voice rather than at the level of content have a faster, cheaper signal about where the conversation actually is, and they get to ask the next question from a different place.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
It is worth slowing down on what Berne was actually proposing, because the model is more careful than the version of it that usually escapes into pop psychology. He was not saying that there is a Parent in your head, an Adult in your head, and a Child in your head, like three little roommates arguing over the dinner table. He was saying that 'Parent,' 'Adult,' and 'Child' are convenient names for three coherent ways an adult human can be at any given moment, three packages of voice, vocabulary, posture, expectation, and bodily tone, and that the package can change inside one conversation without the person changing it on purpose.

The Parent state is everything a person picked up from the authority figures of their early life: the rules they were taught, the shoulds they absorbed, the way those people held their faces when they were disappointed. It comes in two forms. Critical Parent is the version that restricts, judges, and finds fault. Nurturing Parent is the version that takes care, reassures, and soothes. Both are still Parent, and both are still operating from a script written by someone other than the present-tense person speaking. A warm voice telling you what you should feel is not less Parent for being warm; it is just gentler Parent.

Adult is the part that handles what is actually in front of it, right now, with the information it actually has. It is neutral in tone. It is the only state capable of taking in new information without bending it to fit a story already in place. When you change your mind on the basis of something you did not know an hour ago, that is Adult.

Child is the original emotional life of one's own childhood, still alive inside the grown body. Not the cute version. The whole thing: the wanting, the hurt, the curiosity, the cleverness, the old strategies for handling whoever held the authority back then. A person with no access to their Child is not healthier than other people; they are flatter, and usually working very hard to stay that way.

Two things matter most in this part of the chapter, and they matter in opposite directions. The first is that these states are real and observable: you can see one switch on in another person, and on a good day in yourself, before either of you can name it. The second is that the switching is almost never chosen. It is something that happens to a person, not something a person does. That is the part of the model that makes it honest, and it is the part that the next section will hold to its limit.

The chapter does not promise the reader will be able to control which state they speak from next. That is not what the model is designed to do. What it offers instead is a cleaner look at the conversation as it is happening, which is a smaller and more reliable gift than control, and is, on a good day, enough to change what the reader says next.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne's structural model starts with a refusal to flatten the inside of an adult into one thing. The same person, in the same room, in a single five-minute exchange, can be operating from one set of assumptions and reflexes one moment and a completely different set the next, and the change does not require the person to notice it. He proposed that the available sets are three: Parent, Adult, and Child. The names are convenient labels for clusters of voice, vocabulary, posture, expectation, and emotional default.

Parent is the residue of the authority figures of the person's early life. It speaks in rules, judgments, shoulds and shouldn'ts. It has two recognizable faces: Critical Parent restricts and finds fault, while Nurturing Parent protects and reassures. The fact that Nurturing Parent sounds kind does not make it less Parent. It is still the voice of a script learned from somebody else, deployed in the present tense by a person who is not consulting their own current judgment. A line like 'you should be proud of yourself for trying' can be Nurturing Parent doing exactly the same structural work that 'you should know better' does as Critical Parent, just in a softer register.

Adult is the present-tense data-handling state. It observes what is in front of it, evaluates current information, and decides on the basis of the situation actually present rather than the script of past authority or the reaction of past wounds. It is the only state capable of updating beliefs in response to new evidence. It is also the rarest state in conversations that have been going wrong for a while.

Child is what remains, in the grown person, of the original emotional life of their own childhood: the wanting, the hurt, the creativity, the rebellious flicker, the strategies for handling authority that were laid down before the person had words for them. Healthy access to Child is not optional. A person who has lost contact with Child is not more rational; they are flatter, and the access has usually been paid for at a real cost.

Two structural points are doing the work in this chapter, and they cut against each other on purpose. The first is that the states are observable from outside the person. That is what makes the model usable in real time, and is why it is a tool and not a theory. The second is that state shifts are mostly unchosen. They happen in mid-sentence, without permission, and noticing them does not, on its own, switch them off. Both things are true at once, and the next section will hold to that.

The model does not solve the problem of choosing your state. Noticing a state is not the same as switching it, and the chapter does not pretend otherwise. What a clean diagnosis gives the reader is a better next question, not executive control over the ego state that asked the last one. That distinction is the chapter's honest limit.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Pay attention to the seam in Berne's model, because the seam is where most of its leverage lives. He is not making the soft pop-psychology claim that you contain a wise inner adult, a wounded inner child, and a stern inner critic, and that good mental health is about putting the right one in charge. He is making a sharper, less consoling claim: that the inside of a working adult is not one thing, that the available configurations are three, and that the configurations trade off in real time without the person's permission.

Parent is the configuration assembled from the authority figures of the person's early life. It runs on rules, on judgments, on shoulds and shouldn'ts. It has two faces. Critical Parent restricts and finds fault. Nurturing Parent takes care and reassures. Both are still Parent. A warm voice telling someone what they should feel is performing exactly the same structural maneuver as a sharp voice telling them what they should not feel. The maneuver is using a script written by somebody other than the present moment. People who can only hear Parent in its critical face will miss most of the times their nurturing relatives were running it on them.

Adult is the present-tense state: the part that looks at the situation actually in front of it, takes in current information, and is willing to revise its position when the information changes. It is neutral in tone. It is the only configuration capable of new learning. It is also the configuration that disappears first when a conversation stops going well.

Child is the original emotional life of one's own childhood, still active inside a grown body. Not a sanitized inner child. The full inventory: wanting, hurt, curiosity, cleverness, the old reflexes for managing whoever was in charge. Cutting Child off does not make a person more Adult. It usually makes them brittle, and the brittleness costs more than the access would have.

The leverage in the model lives in two facts that point in opposite directions. The first is that the configurations are visible from outside the person. Voice register, vocabulary choice, posture, the kind of reply the speaker is trying to pull from the room: these are all on the outside, which means a sharp observer can read a state shift in real time, before the person experiencing it can. The second is that the shifts themselves are almost never under the speaker's control. They happen mid-sentence, without permission. Noticing one rarely switches it off. The next section is where the chapter pays the price for both of those facts honestly, instead of pretending the model is a remote control.

What the model actually delivers is recognition, not executive function. The reader who treats recognition as the lesser offering has not yet seen how much leverage a half-second of accurate reading provides in a conversation that is already moving fast. Recognition is not the consolation prize. It is what the model was always selling.

activationPrompt.direct: Identify someone in your life whose Parent state shows up in conversation most reliably. Identify the state you most often answer from. The pair is the loop you have been running with them.
activationPrompt.competitive: Pick the relationship in your life that contains the most repeated arguments. Locate the two states that usually meet in those arguments. The pair is the conversation you have been having for years.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: When did you last catch yourself sliding into a state mid-sentence, and what gave you the first warning that the slide was happening?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Name the most recent state shift you noticed in yourself. What was the external marker that tipped you off, before you had a name for it?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Find the last unchosen shift you caught in yourself. Identify the one external signal that gave it away. If you cannot identify the signal, you were not watching closely enough.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: Where in your week does a particular setting, person, or kind of room reliably call up Child in you?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Identify one setting, person, or location that pulls you into Child more often than others do. What about that setting does the pulling?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Name the place that puts you in Child the fastest. Now name what about it does the work. The thing that does the work is what you were going to need to know.

predictionPrompt.gentle: If you started using this model only to notice your own state shifts, and never said the word Parent or Adult to anybody else, what do you think would change in the next two weeks?
predictionPrompt.direct: Predict what you would observe if you used the model exclusively as an internal observation tool, with no external naming, for two weeks. What changes? What does not?
predictionPrompt.competitive: Run the experiment in your head: two weeks of using this model only on yourself, never on anyone else, never as a label. What would change in your conversations? What would stay exactly the same?

retrieve.gentle: Worth understanding: three states (Parent, Adult, Child), each with its own vocabulary and cadence. Parent has both Critical and Nurturing faces, both still Parent. State shifts are mostly unchosen, observable from outside the person, and noticing them does not switch them off.
retrieve.direct: Three states (Parent, Adult, Child), each with its own vocabulary and cadence. Parent has both Critical and Nurturing faces, both still Parent. State shifts are mostly unchosen, observable from outside the person, and noticing them does not switch them off.
retrieve.competitive: Three states (Parent, Adult, Child), each with its own vocabulary and cadence. Parent has both Critical and Nurturing faces, both still Parent. State shifts are mostly unchosen, observable from outside the person, and noticing them does not switch them off. This is the foundation.

connect.gentle: Notice this: recognition is observational, not executive. The leverage comes from a different next question, not from a different state.
connect.direct: Recognition is observational, not executive. The leverage comes from a different next question, not from a different state.
connect.competitive: Recognition is observational, not executive. The leverage comes from a different next question, not from a different state. Know this cold.

preview.gentle: Consider carefully: three voices is the noun list. The next question is what happens when one voice answers another, and why some pairings stabilize a conversation while others derail it.
preview.direct: Three voices is the noun list. The next question is what happens when one voice answers another, and why some pairings stabilize a conversation while others derail it.
preview.competitive: Three voices is the noun list. The next question is what happens when one voice answers another, and why some pairings stabilize a conversation while others derail it. Internalize this now.

examples.title: The last clause of a code review

scenario.gentle: Priya is reviewing Marcus's pull request. She types out a comment. 'This function mutates state on line 42, looks like the bug from last sprint. Could you switch it to return a new object? Also, I don't know why I keep having to explain this.' Marcus reads the comment, hunches a little, and types back, 'Sorry, will fix.' Nothing about the code has changed.
scenario.direct: PRIYA (typing): The function on line 42 mutates state. Same bug pattern as last sprint. Please return a new object instead. (pause) I don't know why I keep having to explain this. MARCUS (reading on his screen, shoulders shifting): Sorry. Will fix it tonight. The first sentence was Adult. The last clause was Parent. Marcus's reply came from Child.
scenario.competitive: Priya's code-review comment ran on rails for two sentences and then derailed in the third. The first two sentences were a senior engineer noticing a bug. The third was a tired teacher who had had enough. Marcus, on the other side of the screen, did not need to be told what had just happened. His shoulders did the math first, his fingers second, and the apology he typed could have been written by a tenth-grader.

whatToDo.gentle: Before sending the next review comment, reread your draft and look at the last clause. If the last clause has changed register from the rest of the comment, delete it. The information was complete by the second sentence.
whatToDo.direct: Treat the last clause of any feedback comment as a state-shift detector. If it sounds like a different person wrote it, the answer is to cut it before sending. Send only the technical content.
whatToDo.competitive: Audit your own outgoing feedback for the late-clause shift before you press send. The cost of a Parent line buried at the end of an Adult comment is not the line itself; it is the way the recipient will read every comment from you for the next month.

whyItMatters.gentle: When a comment shifts register at the end, the recipient remembers the shift, not the content. Cleaning it up before sending keeps the comment doing the work it was meant to do.
whyItMatters.direct: Information in a feedback comment is delivered Adult-to-Adult and read in the register the comment was sent in. A Parent clause changes the read of everything around it.
whyItMatters.competitive: A code review comment is also a relationship. One Parent clause buried at the end is enough to make the reviewer a person to be defended against, not a person to learn from, and that costs every comment that comes after.

scenario.gentle: I had been a manager for nine days when Rebecca, my new direct report, told me she was going to push her deadline by a week. My mouth opened. The voice that came out belonged to my old boss, the one who used to ask 'when do you think this could realistically be done?' in a tone that meant the answer had better be tomorrow. Rebecca's face changed before I had finished the sentence.
scenario.direct: I am nine days into managing a team. Rebecca asks for a one-week extension on a project. Before I form a response from the actual situation in front of me, her workload, the dependencies, what I actually think, a fully formed Parent question arrives in my throat. It is in my old boss's cadence. I hear myself ask it. Rebecca registers the cadence before I do.
scenario.competitive: Nine days into the job. Rebecca walks into our first one-on-one and asks for a one-week extension. I have a chance to be the kind of manager I told myself I was going to be. Instead, an entire sentence in my old boss's voice walks out of my mouth before I can think, and Rebecca's face goes flat in a way I have seen on my own face many times. I am the boss now. The boss is also somebody else.

whatToDo.gentle: Before responding to a request you did not expect, give yourself one breath of silence. In that breath, ask: whose voice is about to come out of my mouth? You will not always be able to redirect it, but the asking buys a small gap.
whatToDo.direct: Insert a five-second pause before your first answer. Use the pause to check whether the voice you are about to use is yours or somebody else's. The pause is the only intervention available, and it works partly.
whatToDo.competitive: Make the silence first. Five seconds. In five seconds you can hear who is about to talk through you. If it is your old boss, you cannot stop them, but you can refuse to send the sentence they wrote and write your own instead.

whyItMatters.gentle: The first one-on-one is the conversation a direct report uses to decide who you are as a manager. A Parent voice in your throat is not the manager you are; it is the manager you had once. Catching it gives the actual you a chance to speak.
whyItMatters.direct: Direct reports calibrate to the voice their manager used the first time they made a request. If that voice was someone else's, the calibration is wrong from the start.
whyItMatters.competitive: Whatever voice you use in the first three of these conversations is the voice your team will assume for the next year. A borrowed Parent voice will buy you a quieter team. Not a candid one.

examples.title: A factual question in Halden's seminar

scenario.gentle: Elena raises her hand in Professor Halden's seminar on Monday afternoon. The question she asks is not a complaint and not a challenge. It is a request: she would like to know what Halden means by the term he has been using for the last fifteen minutes, because she is taking notes and wants to use the term correctly in her paper. Halden hears the question for several seconds before he answers, and when he answers, the answer is not addressed to the request she actually made.
scenario.direct: In Halden's seminar, Elena asks a definitional question about a key term. Adult-to-Adult: tell me what you mean by this so I can use it accurately. Halden takes the question as a challenge to his authority. He answers from Parent, in a register that is half-correction and half-warning. The room registers the mismatch. No one names it.
scenario.competitive: Halden's seminar has fourteen students and an oxygen budget that depends on whether anyone speaks. Elena spends one of her speaking turns asking what Halden means by a term he has been using all hour. It is a clean question. Halden does not hear it as a clean question. He hears it as the kind of question students ask when they are going to be a problem, and his answer is built for that. The cost is not measured in Elena's grade. It is measured in the next eight Mondays of silence.

whatToDo.gentle: If you are the professor and a student's question lands in your Parent, the move is to ask the student to restate the question. Restating it gives both of you a second chance to land it Adult-to-Adult. If you are the student, the move is to write the question down before you ask it next time, and to ask it from the page.
whatToDo.direct: Restate the question yourself before answering. 'Just to make sure I have it: you are asking what I mean by X.' The restate is a state-check disguised as a clarification.
whatToDo.competitive: Restate the question in your own mouth before you answer it. If you cannot restate it without flinching, the flinch is the data; the question landed in Parent. Restate it again from the actual content and answer that one.

whyItMatters.gentle: A professor who answers Adult questions from Parent loses the room slowly, over weeks, in ways nobody complains about and nobody can quite explain. Catching the state shift is the cheapest fix available.
whyItMatters.direct: Seminars are won and lost in the second the instructor decides which state to answer from. The decision is rarely made consciously. Practicing the restate makes it conscious.
whyItMatters.competitive: An instructor who consistently answers Adult questions from Parent has trained the room to stop asking. The damage is invisible until the day there are no questions left, and by then it is too late to find out what the students actually thought.

examples.title: Ms. Alvarez and the marker fight

scenario.gentle: Ms. Alvarez is sitting on a low chair next to two seventh-graders. They have been working on a group project for an hour and are now arguing about whose turn it is to use the markers. The argument is no longer about markers. Ms. Alvarez has watched this happen enough times to know what she is looking at: one of the kids has slipped into a voice that sounds like a tired adult, and the other has slipped into a voice that sounds five years younger than they actually are.
scenario.direct: Ms. Alvarez observes two students in the middle of a group-project conflict. Student A is making rules at Student B in a voice borrowed from a parent. Student B is responding from Child, in a register of grievance. The content is markers. The exchange is Parent-to-Child. Alvarez's job is to give the kids a way to see the exchange without using vocabulary they cannot yet hold.
scenario.competitive: Group projects in seventh grade are a state-shift laboratory. Ms. Alvarez has eight minutes before the bell. Two of her students are locked in a Parent-to-Child loop about markers, and the loop will end in tears or in punishment unless somebody names the loop without naming the theory. She does not have time for theory. She has time for one sentence and one question.

whatToDo.gentle: Sit down at their level. Say: 'I am going to ask both of you a weird question. Right now, do you sound like yourselves, or do you sound like somebody else you know?' Then wait. Let them think about it. Do not solve the markers.
whatToDo.direct: Mirror the voices back to them. 'A minute ago you were both seventh-graders. Right now one of you is a parent and one of you is a five-year-old. Where did you go?' Wait for them to answer. Then ask what they want to do about the markers.
whatToDo.competitive: Cut the content. Hand them the picture instead. 'I want you to listen to your own voices for thirty seconds. Whose voice is it?' If they laugh, you have your opening. If they don't, ask them to swap chairs and try the conversation as themselves again.

whyItMatters.gentle: Twelve-year-olds can absolutely hear when their voices have stopped being their own. They do not have words for it yet. A teacher who asks the right question gives them a memory of the moment they noticed.
whyItMatters.direct: Children pick up the observational use of the model faster than adults do, because they have less invested in being the voice they are using. A teacher who interrupts the loop with a state question is teaching the skill at the right age.
whyItMatters.competitive: A seventh-grader who learns, once, that their voice can stop being theirs in the middle of a sentence has been handed a tool that will quietly save them in twenty conversations a year for the rest of their life. Teachers are the cheapest place this skill can be taught.

scenario.gentle: Looking back at the dishes conversation later that night, Noor could not pinpoint the exact sentence where she had stopped talking about a schedule and started giving a speech. She remembered the proposal: alternating days, she did not mind taking the odd ones, it would take thirty seconds to set up. Then somehow she remembered standing at the counter listing things about responsibility, about how she had grown up, about the kind of person who understood without being told. Chidi had not said anything for a while. The kitchen had felt different, and Noor had not noticed when.
scenario.direct: That night, Noor reconstructs the dishes conversation in her head. The opening was Adult: a clean scheduling proposal. By the third sentence she was no longer in Adult. She was in Parent, giving a speech she could now hear in her mother's cadence. The shift happened in the silence between sentence two and sentence three. She did not decide to make it. The kitchen made it for her, or her mother did from inside her, or both.
scenario.competitive: Noor lay in bed and replayed the kitchen conversation. The clean proposal she had walked in with. The speech she had walked out of. Somewhere between sentence two and sentence three of her own argument, she had stopped being a person solving a sink problem and started being her mother giving a sermon. Chidi had stopped meeting her eyes around sentence four. The next morning was going to be expensive.

whatToDo.gentle: After a conversation that left a strange taste, take five minutes alone and walk back through it sentence by sentence. Try to find the place where the voice you were using stopped sounding like you. Do not use it as evidence against yourself. Use it as a marker for next time.
whatToDo.direct: Reconstruct the conversation backwards, looking only for the moment your register changed. The moment is not always the moment you got loud. Often it is two sentences earlier, and you stopped being in Adult before you stopped being in your own voice.
whatToDo.competitive: Rebuild the conversation in your head, sentence by sentence, until you find the seam. Mark the seam. Next time you are in that room with that person on that topic, you will recognize the seam approaching, and recognizing it is most of what the model gives you.

whyItMatters.gentle: Retroactive recognition is the most common way the model first works on a person. The fix is rarely available in the moment. The marker, laid down at night, is what changes the next morning's conversation.
whyItMatters.direct: Recognition is rarely live. It is mostly retrospective. The retrospective recognition lays down the marker that lets the next conversation be different in small ways the speaker can feel.
whyItMatters.competitive: Couples who can locate the seam after the fact have a different fight available the next time. Couples who cannot locate it are running the same fight in slightly different rooms for years.

scenario.gentle: She is sitting in a low chair in Ms. Alvarez's classroom, the kind of chair that puts your knees up by your chin. Across the table is the teacher, who is calmly explaining that Jamal is doing fine. Danielle's body is sitting in the chair, but her stomach is somewhere in 1996, in the principal's office, waiting for someone to tell her she is in trouble. The teacher has not said anything that warrants this. Danielle notices the gap, and notices that she is about to answer from a place that is not the actual conversation.
scenario.direct: Inner monologue, parent-teacher conference, low chair, strip of construction paper on the wall. Danielle observes her own state: shoulders tense, breathing shallow, the urge to apologize for something Ms. Alvarez has not yet asked her to apologize for. This is Child, called up by the school setting itself. The question Danielle is about to be asked is neutral. The answer she is about to give is going to be from the wrong state.
scenario.competitive: She has been in Ms. Alvarez's classroom for ninety seconds and her body is already a fourteen-year-old's body. The chair is too low. The wall has a strip of tape on it. Ms. Alvarez is being kind. Danielle is ten seconds away from agreeing to whatever the teacher says next, not because she agrees but because Child is the state in the chair and Child agrees to get out of trouble. If she does not interrupt this in the next breath, the next forty minutes will be a parenting conversation she did not have.

whatToDo.gentle: Notice the body first. Adjust your posture in the chair. Take one breath that is longer than the last one. Then ask one neutral question about your child that requires Adult to answer. The question is your way back into the room.
whatToDo.direct: Use a body check as the entry point. Sit straighter, slow your breathing, and ask an Adult-grade question: 'Tell me what you are seeing in his work this term.' Asking from Adult pulls Adult forward. It does not always work; it works often enough.
whatToDo.competitive: Refuse to answer first. Ask. 'Walk me through what you have been seeing this term.' Two things happen. You stop being the one being graded, and you give yourself the ninety seconds you need to climb back into the chair as yourself.

whyItMatters.gentle: Schools call up the Child state in adults more reliably than almost any other setting in life. Knowing that in advance, and having one move ready, gives you a different conference.
whyItMatters.direct: Child reactivation in formal settings is one of the most predictable things the model predicts. Carrying a single, repeatable Adult move into those settings is the most useful self-defense the chapter offers.
whyItMatters.competitive: A parent who walks into a school as Child will agree to interventions they do not believe in, sign forms they did not read, and leave the building feeling smaller than when they came. A parent who carries one Adult question into the room walks out with the same posture they brought in.

questions.prompt: Among Berne's three states, which one is the only one that takes in current information neutrally and is capable of changing its position when new evidence arrives?
choices: Parent
Adult
Child

explanation.gentle: Adult is the present-tense data-handling state. The Parent is busy running rules picked up from somebody else, and the Child is busy running feelings still alive from earlier in your own life. Only Adult is built to update on what is actually in front of it.
explanation.direct: Adult is defined by present-tense observation and the willingness to revise on new evidence. Parent is a script from past authorities and does not update easily. Child is the original emotional life from one's own childhood and reacts before evaluating.
explanation.competitive: Updating on new evidence is the move only Adult can make. Parent will try to fit the new evidence into the script it already has. Child will react to the evidence before reading it.

questions.prompt: In the code review where Priya leaves a comment on Marcus's pull request, what is the marker that her state has shifted by the end of the comment?
choices: Marcus replies more slowly than usual
The technical content of the comment changes from the first sentence to the last
The register of the last clause is different from the rest of the comment, and Marcus's body answers the change before he does

explanation.gentle: The shift is in the register, not the content. Marcus's hunched shoulders are the early signal because the body picks up the new voice before the conscious mind names it. A slower reply happens, but it happens downstream of the shift.
explanation.direct: Register change is the marker; the content of the technical note stayed the same. Body language is the early signal because state shifts move faster than vocabulary. A slower reply is a consequence, not the marker.
explanation.competitive: Register, not content, is the move you are looking for. The technical note Priya wrote does not change in information; it changes in voice. A reply that comes more slowly is downstream of that change, not evidence of it.

questions.prompt: A senior colleague says, in a warm and encouraging tone, 'You should feel really proud of yourself for trying.' Which state is this most likely coming from?
choices: Parent (specifically Nurturing Parent)
Adult
Child

explanation.gentle: Warmth does not move a line out of Parent. The 'should' is a rule about what someone is supposed to feel, and rules about feeling are still Parent territory, just in their kinder face.
explanation.direct: Nurturing Parent is the kind face of the same script. The word 'should' tied to a feeling is the marker; an Adult observation about the same situation would describe what happened, not prescribe the response.
explanation.competitive: Look at the verb. 'Should feel' is a Parent prescription dressed in nurturing tone. An Adult observation would describe rather than instruct. The tone is kind; the move is still Parent.

questions.prompt: Sam, nine days into managing a new team, hears a sentence in his old boss's cadence walk out of his own mouth during a one-on-one with Rebecca. Of the following, which move is the chapter actually recommending?
choices: Apologize aloud for using the wrong tone and start the sentence over
Insert a brief silence before the next answer and use it to check whose voice is about to come out
Decide in advance to be the Adult and trust that decision to hold

explanation.gentle: Inserting a small silence is the only move the chapter actually claims will work, and it only works partly. Apologizing on the spot can make the moment more about Sam than about Rebecca, and deciding to be Adult is exactly the kind of remote-control move the chapter says the model does not give you.
explanation.direct: A short pause before the next response is the realistic intervention because it interrupts the script long enough to check it. Apologizing in the moment escalates self-focus. 'Deciding to be Adult' is the move the chapter explicitly says is unavailable, because state shifts are not under will.
explanation.competitive: Five seconds of silence is the move the chapter actually backs. Apologizing on the spot puts the manager at the center of a conversation that should still be about the report. Willing yourself into Adult is the failure mode the chapter spends its hard-depth section refusing to promise.

questions.prompt: When Professor Halden answers Elena's factual question as if it were a challenge, the most accurate description of what happened is:
choices: Halden was rude and Elena's question deserved a better answer
Elena's question was unclear and prompted a defensive answer
Elena's question was sent from Adult and Halden's answer came back from Parent, and the room felt the mismatch even though no one named it

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not making a moral claim about Halden. It is describing a state mismatch: Elena asked from Adult, and Halden answered from Parent. Calling him rude misses the structural point and does not give the reader a tool. Saying the question was unclear is a story about Elena, not about the exchange.
explanation.direct: Mismatch between sending state and answering state is the diagnosis the chapter is offering. 'Rude' is a moral label that does not tell the reader anything they can use. 'Unclear question' is a story that locates the problem in the wrong person.
explanation.competitive: Mismatch of states is the diagnosis. Rudeness is a label, and it gives you nothing to do next. Blaming the question lets the listener off the hook for the state they answered from. Naming the mismatch gives you a tool for the next class.

questions.prompt: Danielle notices, in the low chair at her son's parent-teacher conference, that her body has slipped into Child. According to the chapter, what does noticing this give her?
choices: A place to stand and a different question to ask next, but not a guaranteed escape from the Child state itself
An immediate exit from Child once she names it
Permission to apologize to Ms. Alvarez for being defensive

explanation.gentle: The chapter is careful here. Noticing is observational, not executive. Danielle does not get to leave the state by recognizing it. What she gets is a small gap in which she can ask the next question from a slightly different place. That is the smaller, more honest claim the model makes.
explanation.direct: Recognition gives location, not control. The state does not lift on being named. The gap between recognition and reaction is where the next move can come from, and that gap is most of what the model offers a person. A preemptive apology is its own state move, not a fix.
explanation.competitive: Recognition gives Danielle a place to stand. It does not give her a switch. The honest version of the chapter is that the state stays for a while and the person gets to ask a different question from inside it. Anyone selling her an exit from Child by naming it is selling something the model does not contain.

questions.prompt: A customer-service agent on a call answers an angry customer's reasonable question with a scripted line that begins, 'Sir, you need to understand...'. Which state is the agent operating from at that moment?
choices: Adult
Child
Parent

explanation.gentle: The phrase 'you need to understand' is a rule directed at someone else, which puts it in Parent. An Adult response would describe the actual policy or the actual situation. A Child response would react to the customer's anger emotionally, often defensively.
explanation.direct: 'You need to understand' is a Parent move because it is a rule about how the other person should be in this conversation. Adult would handle the substance. Child would react to the anger.
explanation.competitive: Watch the verb. 'You need to' is rule-issuing. Rule-issuing belongs to Parent. The agent is not yet handling the customer's question; they are positioning the customer in the room. Adult would address content. Child would absorb the anger.

questions.prompt: Noor, the morning after the dishes conversation with Chidi, wants to do something useful with the recognition that her state had shifted. Which next question is the chapter actually recommending?
choices: How can I be more Adult in our next conversation?
What was actually happening in the kitchen last night, including which voices were in the room?
How can I get Chidi to recognize that he was being defensive?

explanation.gentle: The chapter explicitly redirects from 'how do I win the argument' to 'what was actually happening in the room.' That second question is what observation buys you. The first question treats the model as a self-improvement tool, and the third treats it as a way to label other people, which is the misuse the chapter warns against.
explanation.direct: Locating what happened, including the voices present, is the use of recognition the chapter argues for. 'How can I be more Adult' is the executive misreading the chapter spends its limit-paragraph correcting. 'How do I get Chidi to recognize' is the diagnose-the-other-person misuse.
explanation.competitive: 'What was actually happening' is the question the chapter pays for. 'Be more Adult' is the move the chapter says you cannot make. Diagnosing Chidi is the move the chapter explicitly does not support, because the model is not for labeling other people's behavior at them.

questions.prompt: If the model cannot let a reader will themselves into Adult, why does the chapter argue it is still worth using?
choices: Because recognition gives the reader a different question to ask next, and a different question leads to a different conversation, even when the state itself does not lift
Because the model is more accurate than other psychological frameworks
Because labeling other people's states gives the reader leverage in conflicts

explanation.gentle: The chapter's smaller, honest claim is that the model gives you a place to stand and a different question to ask. That different question is what changes the next conversation, not the state itself. Accuracy claims are not what the chapter argues, and using the model on other people is exactly the misuse it warns against.
explanation.direct: Recognition opens a different question. A different question is what the model trades for the lack of an executive switch. The chapter does not make accuracy claims about the model relative to other frameworks. It explicitly rejects using the model to label other people.
explanation.competitive: Different question, different conversation. That is the trade. Accuracy claims are not what the chapter is selling. Using the model as a labeling weapon is the failure mode the chapter is built to refuse.

questions.prompt: If naming a state cannot make a reader choose it, what does the chapter say noticing is actually for?
choices: For locating the state honestly, so the next move comes from a different place than the last move did
For gradually retraining the brain to default to Adult
For developing an internal scoreboard of how often each state shows up

explanation.gentle: The chapter calls this 'locating.' Once you know which voice was actually in the room, the question you ask next is different, and the answer you give next comes from somewhere different too. The chapter does not promise gradual retraining, and it does not propose the model as a counting tool.
explanation.direct: Locating is the word the chapter uses. Noticing is for finding where the conversation actually was, so the next move is not the same move. There is no claim of gradual retraining and no scoreboard model in the chapter.
explanation.competitive: Locate the state. That is the use. The next move comes from a different place because it has a different starting point. Retraining is not what the chapter promises, and treating the model as a scoreboard turns it into the diagnostic tool the chapter explicitly tells you it is not.

coreSkill.gentle: The core skill here is identifying which of the three ego states — Parent, Adult, or Child — is active in yourself during live conversation, before responding.
coreSkill.direct: Identifying which of the three ego states — Parent, Adult, or Child — is active in yourself during live conversation, before responding.
coreSkill.competitive: Master this: identifying which of the three ego states — Parent, Adult, or Child — is active in yourself during live conversation, before responding.

plan.gentle: When this comes up, consider: if you notice a shift in register mid-sentence — yours or someone else's — then hold the observation without naming it and ask your next question from a different place than your reflex would have.
plan.direct: If you notice a shift in register mid-sentence — yours or someone else's — then hold the observation without naming it and ask your next question from a different place than your reflex would have.
plan.competitive: In this situation, act immediately: if you notice a shift in register mid-sentence — yours or someone else's — then hold the observation without naming it and ask your next question from a different place than your reflex would have.

plan.gentle: When this comes up, consider: if you hear yourself slide from Adult into Parent or Child in the middle of a conversation, then write down the seam afterward in one sentence — not as judgment, as a marker.
plan.direct: If you hear yourself slide from Adult into Parent or Child in the middle of a conversation, then write down the seam afterward in one sentence — not as judgment, as a marker.
plan.competitive: In this situation, act immediately: if you hear yourself slide from Adult into Parent or Child in the middle of a conversation, then write down the seam afterward in one sentence — not as judgment, as a marker.

twentyFourHourChallenge.gentle: For the next 24 hours: in the next 24 hours, in three conversations, try to identify which state you ended each sentence in — not the other person's, yours.

chapters.title: What a Transaction Is and Why They Go Wrong

chapterBreakdown.gentle: You already know what it feels like when somebody asks you a normal question and you accidentally answer it from a place that has nothing to do with what they asked. Tomas asks Aiya whether the API change is going to land Friday, and Aiya answers in a tone that says she is tired of explaining things to him. The question was clean. The answer arrived in a different room. Berne built a small picture for what just happened. Every exchange is two arrows: one from the speaker, one back from the listener. When the second arrow lands where the first one was waiting for it, the conversation is stable and can continue. When it lands somewhere else, the conversation breaks in the second sentence and most of the people in the room feel the break before they can name it. Most stalled meetings and most stalled phone calls are crossed in exactly this way.
chapterBreakdown.direct: A transaction is the smallest unit Berne's model handles: one person sends a message, the other sends one back. Each message comes from one ego state and is aimed at another ego state. When the response comes from the state that was addressed and is aimed back at the sender state, the transaction is complementary, and the conversation is stable. When the response comes from a different state, or is aimed somewhere else, the transaction is crossed, and the conversation breaks in the second exchange. Most communication failures that feel personal are not personal. They are crossed transactions, and they have a shape on a page: two arrows that did not line up. The work is to draw the two arrows in your head in real time and to read, before either person has the vocabulary for it, whether the arrows line up or whether they cross.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: In any conversation that has gone wrong on you, the cost was almost certainly paid in the second exchange. Somebody sent a message from one ego state aimed at another. The reply did not come from where it was supposed to come from, and the conversation derailed in the time it takes a sentence to land. Berne built a notation for that exact failure mode. Two arrows on a page: one from the speaker's state, one back from the listener's state. When the arrows line up, the exchange is complementary and the meeting can run for an hour. When they cross, the meeting changes shape inside two sentences and nobody in the room can quite say why. Reading the cross before anyone in the room has the vocabulary for it is the cheapest leverage you have in a stalled conversation, and the most reliable.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Once you have the three voices in your head, the next thing the model gives you is a way to draw what happens between voices. Berne's word for the smallest unit of social exchange is transaction. Two messages: one out, one back. The picture you can draw of any transaction is two arrows. The first arrow leaves the sender from one of their three states and points at one of the receiver's three states. The second arrow does the same thing in reverse. The whole question is whether the two arrows line up.

When the arrows line up, the exchange is complementary. The response comes from the state the sender was addressing, and it aims back at the state the sender sent from. Coach Reyes meets Diego on the pool deck, towel around his shoulders, and offers him the soothing line that nurturing coaches have offered after bad races forever. Reyes is in Nurturing Parent, talking to Diego's Adapted Child. Diego thanks him, from his Adapted Child, talking back to Reyes's Nurturing Parent. Both arrows are parallel. The exchange is stable. It could be repeated after every bad race for four years and never break. The trap to avoid is the easy reading that complementary means good. Stable is not good. A long-running complementary loop on the wrong vector can run for years and serve neither person.

When the arrows do not line up, the exchange is crossed. The response comes from a state the sender did not address, or it aims back at a state the sender was not in, or both. Olivia called Kenji asking, from her Child, for Kenji's Parent to soothe her. Kenji answered from her Adult: 'What specifically happened on Tuesday?' The arrows crossed inside two sentences. Both sisters are technically right, and the call ended with a small wound that will not be discussed next week. Crossed transactions are not anyone's moral failure. They are an alignment problem with the arrows. The arrow is the diagnostic, not the accusation.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne calls the smallest unit of social exchange a transaction. A transaction has two parts: a stimulus and a response. The stimulus comes from one of the speaker's three ego states and is aimed at one of the listener's three ego states. The response is the same kind of vector in reverse. He proposed that you can draw any transaction as two arrows on a single picture, and that whether the arrows line up or cross is the central diagnostic question.

When the response comes from the state the stimulus addressed, and is aimed back at the state the stimulus came from, the transaction is complementary. The arrows are parallel. Adult to Adult, Adult back. Parent to Child, Child back. Child to Parent, Parent back. Complementary transactions are stable: they can continue indefinitely on the same vector because expectations are met on both sides. The error to avoid is the moral one. Stable is not good. A coach and a thirteen-year-old swimmer can run a Nurturing Parent to Adapted Child loop for four years after every bad race, and that loop is complementary, and it can also be exactly the conversation that prevents the swimmer from ever asking whether he wants to keep swimming.

When the response comes from a different state than the one the stimulus addressed, or is aimed at a different state than the sender's, the transaction is crossed. The arrows do not line up. The conversation breaks in the second exchange, almost always before either party has the vocabulary for what happened. A late-night phone call between sisters illustrates the cleanest version: one sister calls Child-to-Parent for comfort, the other answers Adult-to-Adult with a clarifying question, and the call ends with a small unspoken wound. Both sisters are technically right. The exchange crossed because the two arrows did not align, and that is what the diagram is built to show. Getting the diagram right, even once, is worth the read. That distinction is the chapter's essential claim.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The reason most stalled conversations stay stalled is that the people inside them are still arguing about content when the actual problem is structural. Berne's contribution to that problem was a small notation. He proposed that any single exchange between two people can be drawn as two arrows. The first arrow leaves the speaker from one of three ego states and points at one of the listener's three. The second arrow does the same thing in reverse. The whole leverage of the model lives in whether the second arrow lands where the first one was waiting for it.

When it does, the transaction is complementary, and the conversation is stable. The conversation can continue on that vector for an hour, a meeting, four years of swim practice. The trap to refuse is the soft reading: that complementary is the same thing as good. It is not. Two people can run a Nurturing-Parent-to-Adapted-Child loop after every bad race for years and never have the conversation that one of them actually needs. Stability is a fact about the bones of the exchange, not a value judgment about whether the exchange is doing useful work.

When the arrows do not line up, the transaction is crossed, and the conversation breaks in the second exchange. The break is faster than vocabulary. People feel it before they can describe it. A clean example: one sister calls another asking, from her Child, to be soothed by the other's Parent. The other sister answers from her Adult, with a sharp clarifying question. The call ends with a residue both sisters will pretend they did not notice. Both are technically right. The exchange crossed because the second arrow did not land where the first one was aimed, and the diagram is the only place that fact has anywhere to go. Reading the cross before anyone else in the room can name it is the cheapest leverage available in a conversation that is already going wrong. That leverage compounds.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The three voices alone are not enough. Once you can hear which state somebody is speaking from, the next question is the relational one: what just happened between their state and yours? Berne's answer was to give us a notation small enough to use in a real conversation. He called the unit a transaction. The notation is two arrows. The first arrow leaves the sender from one ego state and points at one ego state in the receiver. The second arrow does the same thing in reverse. The whole question, every time, is whether the two arrows line up.

When they line up, the exchange is complementary. The response comes from the state the stimulus was addressed to, and it aims back at the state the stimulus came from. Adult to Adult, Adult back. Parent to Child, Child back. Child to Parent, Parent soothing. Complementary transactions are stable. They can run on the same vector indefinitely because both people are getting the kind of reply they were unconsciously expecting. The trap most readers fall into here is the easy moral reading: complementary is good, crossed is bad. The chapter cannot let you have that reading. A swim coach and a thirteen-year-old can run a Nurturing-Parent-to-Adapted-Child exchange after every bad race for four years and have a complementary, stable loop that never once has the conversation the boy actually needs about whether he wants to keep swimming. Stability is a fact about the bones of an exchange, not a verdict about whether the exchange is doing the work that needed doing.

When the arrows do not line up, the transaction is crossed. The response comes from a different state, or aims at a different state, or both. The conversation breaks in the second sentence, faster than vocabulary. The clearest version is small and sad: a phone call between two sisters where one is asking, from her Child, for the other's Parent to soothe her, and the other answers from her Adult with a clarifying question. Both are technically right. Both are also in different conversations now, and the call ends with a residue that will not be mentioned next week. The diagram does not blame either sister. It just shows that the second arrow did not land where the first one was aimed.

Two things have to survive into the rest of the chapter, and they cut against each other on purpose. The first is that complementary and crossed are real, observable, and diagrammable in real time. The second is that drawing the diagram does not tell you what to do about the cross. The diagram is a diagnosis, not a prescription. The next section will pay the price for that distinction honestly, by showing that the same diagnosed cross can have three different right answers depending on what the person actually wants from the conversation. The cross is only the beginning of the question. The chapter's structure ends there deliberately.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne's structural contribution after the three states was a notation for what happens between states. He called the unit of exchange a transaction. A transaction has two parts: a stimulus, sent from one of the speaker's three ego states and aimed at one of the listener's three, and a response, which is the same kind of vector in reverse. The notation is two arrows on a single picture. The diagnostic question, every time, is whether the second arrow lands where the first one expected it.

The complementary case is the case where it does. The response comes from the state the stimulus addressed, and aims back at the state the stimulus came from. The arrows are parallel. Adult to Adult, Adult back. Parent to Child, Child back. Child to Parent, Parent soothing. Complementary transactions are stable in the technical sense that the exchange can be repeated indefinitely without breaking, because both people are receiving the reply their state was unconsciously demanding. The reader's first temptation is to translate stability as goodness. The chapter must refuse that translation. A nurturing coach and a thirteen-year-old swimmer can run a Nurturing-Parent-to-Adapted-Child exchange after every bad race for four years, and the exchange is fully complementary, fully stable, and exactly the conversation that prevents the swimmer from ever raising the question of whether he wants to keep racing. Stability describes the bones, not the value.

The crossed case is the case where the second arrow does not land. The response comes from a different state than the one addressed, or aims at a different state than the one that sent the stimulus, or both. The conversation breaks in the second exchange, almost always faster than the participants can vocabulary it. The cleanest example is structural: one sister calls another asking, from Child, for the other's Parent to soothe her. The second sister answers from Adult with a clarifying question. The arrows crossed in the second sentence. Both sisters are technically right. The call ends with a residue that will not be discussed next week. The diagram is silent on whose fault the cross was, because the diagram is not a tool for assigning fault.

Two structural facts must survive together into hard depth. The first is that complementary and crossed are observable and diagrammable in real time. The second is that the diagram is diagnostic only. Knowing that the second arrow crossed does not tell the reader which of three available responses is the right one: deliberately recrossing (sending an Adult arrow back into the other person's Parent and refusing to play the assigned Child role), accepting the cross and naming it ('there is a different conversation we need to have first'), or doing nothing in the moment and using the recognition to walk into the next instance of the same exchange differently. Each is sometimes the right answer, and the model itself does not pick. Neither move is right by default; both are right in context.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Pay attention to the seam in this chapter, because the seam is what separates a useful tool from a useless one. The first half teaches a notation: every transaction has a sender state, a receiver state, and a return vector, and the whole picture lives in whether the return vector lands where the original arrow was waiting for it. The second half teaches the limit of the notation, which is what most readers will need most.

When the return vector lands where it was expected, the exchange is complementary, and the conversation is stable on that vector. Adult-to-Adult requests met by Adult-to-Adult answers run sprints. Parent-to-Child instructions met by Child compliance run institutions. Child-to-Parent appeals met by Parent comfort run families. Stability, in this sense, is a structural fact about the bones of the exchange. It is not a verdict on what the exchange is doing for either party. A swim coach and a thirteen-year-old can run a four-year Nurturing-Parent-to-Adapted-Child loop after every bad race in which both arrows always line up, and that loop works perfectly as a transaction and prevents the conversation the boy actually needs about whether he still wants to be in the pool.

When the return vector misses, the exchange is crossed, and the conversation breaks in the time it takes a sentence to land. The cleanest version is small and sad: one sister calls another asking, from her Child, for the other's Parent to soothe her, and the other sister answers from her Adult with a clarifying question. Both are technically right, and the call ends with a residue neither of them will mention next week. The diagram is silent on whose fault the cross was, because fault is not what the diagram is built to compute.

The leverage in the chapter, and the reason it has to come second in the book and not first, is the limit. Drawing the cross gives the reader a diagnosis. It does not give them a prescription. The diagnosed cross has at least three available answers, and the diagram does not pick. The first is to recross deliberately, sending an Adult arrow back into the other person's Parent and refusing to play the assigned Child role. The second is to accept the cross and name it openly: 'there is a different conversation we need to have first.' The third is to do nothing in the moment and use the recognition to walk into the next instance differently. Each is the right answer in some setting. A reader who wants the diagram to also pick for them is asking the model to do work the model is not built to do, and will be disappointed in exactly the way last chapter's reader was disappointed when noticing a state did not let them choose it. The chapter's honest reach ends at diagnosis. The reader who waits for the model to choose the move has misread what the model was built to provide.

activationPrompt.gentle: Bring to mind a recurring conversation in your life that always seems to end in the same place. Think of it as a series of arrow pairs that keep crossing in the same way, and see if you can find the recurring cross.
activationPrompt.direct: Identify a recurring conversation in your life that ends the same way every time. The pattern is a recurring cross. Locate the cross point: which state in you keeps sending, and which state in them keeps answering.
activationPrompt.competitive: Pick the conversation in your life that you have already had four times this year and will have again. The pattern is a recurring crossed transaction. Find the recurring cross point. The cross point is the conversation you are not having.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: When did you most recently catch yourself deliberately recrossing a transaction, and what made you choose to recross instead of accepting it or waiting?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Name the last time you recrossed a transaction on purpose. What told you that recrossing was the right move rather than naming or waiting?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Find the most recent deliberate recross you made. Name the signal that told you it was the right move and not naming or waiting. If you cannot find one, you have been defaulting to one of the three moves without choosing.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: Where in your life do you most often run a stable complementary loop that is not actually serving you?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Identify a stable complementary loop in your life that has been running for years and is crowding out a conversation you have been avoiding.
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Name the longest-running stable complementary loop in your life. Now name the conversation it has been preventing. The loop is doing work; the question is whether the work is the work you want done.

predictionPrompt.gentle: If, for the next two weeks, you tried to draw the two arrows of every important conversation in your head before responding, what would you predict you would notice that you do not currently notice?
predictionPrompt.direct: Predict what would change if you spent two weeks deliberately drawing the two arrows of each important exchange in your head before responding. What would you start to see?
predictionPrompt.competitive: Run the experiment in your head: two weeks of consciously drawing the two arrows in your head before answering. What conversations would change? What would stay the same? What pattern that you have been calling personal would turn out to be structural?
