scenario.gentle: It is Tuesday morning stand-up. Five people are on the call. Tomas types a status into chat and then unmutes. 'Aiya, is the API change going to land Friday or do I need to push the release notes?' Aiya unmutes and waits a beat. 'Tomas, we have been over this. The dependency on the auth service hasn't changed since last week.' Tomas's face does something he did not authorize. The other four people on the call look at the screen and wait.
scenario.direct: TOMAS (Adult to Adult): Aiya, is the API change going to land Friday, or do I need to push the release notes? AIYA (Parent to Child, with a quarter-inch of disappointment): Tomas, we have been over this. The dependency on the auth service hasn't changed since last week. The arrows crossed in the second exchange. The next ten minutes belong to a different meeting.
scenario.competitive: Tomas asked a clean question on a Tuesday stand-up. Aiya answered in a tone that took the question as evidence of his incompetence. Two sentences in, the meeting was no longer about the API change, and the four other people on the call were watching to see what Tomas would do with his face. The rest of stand-up cost his team forty minutes.

whatToDo.gentle: Notice the cross before you respond. Take one breath. Then ask one clean Adult question that returns to the original content: 'Just to be sure I have it, is the auth dependency still where it was last week?' The Adult question is not a fix for Aiya's Parent. It is a way to keep your own arrow where you wanted it.
whatToDo.direct: Recross deliberately. Send an Adult question back into Aiya's Parent and refuse the Child role she just assigned you. 'The question I am asking is whether the auth dependency moved this week.' The recross does not soothe Aiya. It refuses the role.
whatToDo.competitive: Recross. Send a clean Adult arrow back into her Parent and refuse the Child role. The line is short: 'The question is whether the dependency moved this week.' The other four people on the call will register the recross before Aiya does, and the meeting will move.

whyItMatters.gentle: Crossed transactions in stand-ups cost more than the meeting they happen in. The team learns to read the room as Tomas's-meeting-just-went-sideways and starts bracing for it. Catching the cross in real time and recrossing prevents the team from learning the wrong pattern.
whyItMatters.direct: Group meetings calibrate to the second arrow. If the second arrow stands, the team learns that this is the room Tomas operates in. A clean recross teaches the room the opposite.
whyItMatters.competitive: A meeting where the project manager visibly takes a Parent hit and answers from Child has changed shape for the team that watched it. The pattern is not local. It will show up in the next four meetings unless the recross teaches the room to expect a different second arrow.

examples.title: Mei, Devi, and the triage policy

scenario.gentle: In the customer support stand-up at a small SaaS company, the lead engineer Mei asks Devi, the most junior on the team, a routine question: 'Did the new ticket triage policy slow you down yesterday?' Devi hears it as criticism, not as a question, and answers from somewhere small. 'I did my best.' Mei did not mean it as criticism. The room knows Mei did not mean it as criticism. The room also watches Devi go quiet for the rest of the stand-up.
scenario.direct: Stand-up. Mei (lead engineer, Adult to Adult): Did the new triage policy slow you down yesterday? Devi (junior, Adapted Child): I did my best. Mei's question was an information request. Devi's answer was an apology to a Parent that Mei was not. The room registers the cross. Nobody names it. Devi does not speak again until end of stand-up.
scenario.competitive: Mei asked Devi a clean Adult question about the new triage policy. Devi heard a Parent. Devi answered from her Adapted Child with an apology Mei did not need and could not redirect, and the rest of the stand-up was conducted around a junior engineer who had stopped being present in it. Mei's three sentences trying to fix it later did not land, because the room had already filed the cross and moved on without her.

whatToDo.gentle: Mei's best move is not to apologize for asking. It is to address Devi's actual answer, gently, after stand-up. 'When you said you did your best, what did you hear me ask?' That question, asked alone, gives Devi a chance to bring her Adult back into the conversation.
whatToDo.direct: After stand-up, take Devi aside. Ask: 'What did you hear me asking in there?' The question pulls Devi out of Adapted Child by treating her as the person who can answer it. Apologizing for the original question keeps the Parent role in the room.
whatToDo.competitive: Pull Devi aside after stand-up. One question: 'What did you hear me asking?' The question is the recross, not the apology. The apology keeps you in the Parent seat. The question hands the seat back.

whyItMatters.gentle: Junior engineers calibrate quickly to the question of whether their lead is a Parent or an Adult. The first crossed transaction usually does not break the relationship. The third one does.
whyItMatters.direct: Adapted Child responses to Adult questions are how juniors learn to stop volunteering information. The cost is not the meeting; it is the next month of meetings, when the junior is quieter and slower.
whyItMatters.competitive: A team where juniors answer Adult questions from Adapted Child is a team that has stopped reporting information. Mei's job in the next forty-eight hours is not to apologize. It is to make the next exchange a clean Adult-to-Adult one.

examples.title: Coach Reyes on the pool deck

scenario.gentle: Coach Reyes meets Diego on the pool deck after the boy's slowest 200 free of the season. The towel is around Diego's shoulders. The chlorine is still in the air. Reyes says, in a tone that has been carrying boys through bad races for fifteen years, 'It's okay, Diego. You swam your best.' Diego says, 'Thanks, Coach.' The exchange is over in five seconds. Both of them have done it before. Both of them will do it again next week.
scenario.direct: REYES (Nurturing Parent to Adapted Child): It's okay, Diego. You swam your best. DIEGO (Adapted Child to Nurturing Parent): Thanks, Coach. Two parallel arrows. Complementary. Stable. Repeatable. Exactly the conversation Diego does not need.
scenario.competitive: Reyes and Diego have run this exchange after every bad race for two seasons. Reyes from Nurturing Parent, Diego from Adapted Child, both arrows lined up like a chord chart. The exchange is stable. The exchange is also the reason Diego has not asked, in two years, whether he wants to keep swimming. The conversation that would matter has been crowded out of the pool deck by the conversation that always works.

whatToDo.gentle: Reyes can break the loop by sending the next message from Adult instead of Nurturing Parent. 'Diego, can you tell me what you noticed in the second fifty?' That question treats Diego as someone who has data, which pulls his Adult forward and gives him a different state to answer from.
whatToDo.direct: Replace the Nurturing Parent line with an Adult question. 'What did you notice in the second fifty?' The question is the same recross move from earlier in the chapter, applied to a complementary loop instead of a crossed one. Stability gets broken on purpose.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop running the loop. Send Adult next time: 'Tell me what you saw in the second fifty.' The question deliberately crosses the complementary vector you have both been running for two years. The cross is the point. It is the only way the actual conversation gets a chance to start.

whyItMatters.gentle: Stable conversations are not the same as useful ones. A complementary loop that prevents the conversation that matters is a structural problem, not a relationship problem, and it is fixed by changing the state the loop runs on.
whyItMatters.direct: Long-running complementary loops on the wrong vector are how relationships avoid the conversations that would matter most. Breaking the loop intentionally is the move that lets the avoided conversation become available.
whyItMatters.competitive: A coach who runs the same complementary line after every bad race for two years has trained the swimmer to never bring the actual question into the pool deck. The cost is not visible until the swimmer quits, and by then the loop is the only conversation either of them knows how to have.

scenario.gentle: I was sitting in Mara's office for our biweekly thesis meeting. She was looking at the chapter I had submitted, with the highlighter still in her hand from her own margin notes. She asked me, 'Yusuf, what is this paragraph trying to do?' It was a clean Adult question. Before I could form an Adult answer, I heard myself say, 'I'm sorry, I know it's not working.' The 'I'm sorry' was not from where the question had been aimed. I had crossed my own conversation in the middle of it.
scenario.direct: Mara's office. Open thesis chapter on her desk, highlighter in her hand. Mara (Adult to Adult): Yusuf, what is this paragraph trying to do? Me (Adapted Child to a Nurturing Parent that I had just constructed inside my own head): I'm sorry, I know it's not working. I crossed my own transaction. Mara had not been in Parent. I built one for her so I could answer from Child.
scenario.competitive: Two minutes into the meeting Mara asked me what the paragraph was trying to do. It was the cleanest Adult question she had asked me in a year. I answered from a place that had nothing to do with what she had asked, and I did it in a tone that constructed her as a parent who was disappointed in me. She had not been disappointed. I had built her disappointment into the room and then answered to it. By the time I noticed, I had spent the rest of the meeting apologizing for things she had not asked me to apologize for.

whatToDo.gentle: When you catch yourself crossing your own transaction, the first move is the same one from chapter one: notice. Do not apologize for the apology. Take a breath, then return to the original question. 'Let me try again. What the paragraph is trying to do is...' The restate is the recross.
whatToDo.direct: Restate the question and answer the actual one. 'Let me try that again. The paragraph is trying to argue X.' The restate refuses the Parent you constructed and pulls you back into Adult. Apologizing for the apology compounds the cross.
whatToDo.competitive: Restate. 'Let me try again. The paragraph is trying to argue X.' Anything else extends the cross you started. The advisor was not in Parent until you put her there, and the only way out of the room you built is to walk back to the original question.

whyItMatters.gentle: Crossing your own transaction is a real category, and it is more common than crossing somebody else's. Catching it is harder because the Parent you are answering to is one you built. The fix is the same: return to the original question.
whyItMatters.direct: Self-crossed transactions are the hardest to spot because the Parent role is being played by a hallucinated version of the listener. The fix is mechanical: restate the original question and answer it.
whyItMatters.competitive: Apologizing for things nobody asked you to apologize for is a state move, not a kindness. The move builds a Parent that was not in the room and then answers to it. The cost is two years of meetings where the advisor never got the answer she actually asked for, and where you never got the meeting you actually came to have.

scenario.gentle: It is 9:47 on a Tuesday night. The phone is propped against the salt shaker on the kitchen counter. Olivia called Kenji because the week had been bad and she wanted to be told that everything was going to be okay. Kenji has just asked, 'What specifically happened on Tuesday?' Olivia hears the question and feels her mouth start to answer it, and feels something else in her chest get smaller. The question is reasonable. Kenji is reasonable. Olivia is going to be off the phone in about four minutes, and tomorrow she is going to wonder why she didn't call somebody else.
scenario.direct: 9:47 PM. Phone on the counter. Inner monologue: Olivia just sent a Child-to-Parent appeal for comfort. Kenji answered from Adult. Olivia recognizes the cross in real time. The question 'What specifically happened on Tuesday?' is a perfectly fine Adult question; it is not the conversation Olivia called for. She has about thirty seconds to decide whether to answer Kenji's question, name the cross, or hang up sooner than planned.
scenario.competitive: 9:47 PM. Olivia called for one reason and her sister has answered as if the call were about a different reason. The Adult question is technically correct. The Adult question is also the conversation that ends the call early and leaves Olivia to spend Wednesday wondering why she does not feel called back. She has thirty seconds to choose whether the next sentence she sends is the answer to the question, or the conversation she actually came for.

whatToDo.gentle: Olivia can name the cross, gently. 'I'm not really looking for a postmortem on Tuesday. I'm just having a hard week and I wanted to hear your voice.' That sentence does what the diagram cannot: it tells Kenji which conversation is in the room.
whatToDo.direct: Name the cross out loud. 'I am not looking for a postmortem. I am having a hard week and wanted to hear your voice.' Naming the cross tells Kenji which arrow Olivia actually sent and gives Kenji a chance to send a different one back.
whatToDo.competitive: Name it. 'I am not looking for a postmortem. I am having a bad week and I wanted to hear your voice.' Anything less specific lets Kenji answer the wrong question for another five minutes and lets Olivia walk into Wednesday wondering whose fault the call was.

whyItMatters.gentle: Naming the cross is the second of the three moves the chapter offers. It does not always work. It works often enough that it is worth knowing as the first available answer when recrossing feels like asking for a fight.
whyItMatters.direct: Naming the cross is a structural intervention. It tells the other person which arrow you actually sent and asks them to send a different one back. It works when the relationship can hold the request and not when it cannot.
whyItMatters.competitive: The unspoken cost of an unnamed cross between two close people is paid in the next four phone calls neither of them quite makes. Naming it converts the residue into a question both people can answer.

examples.title: Bea walks back the Saturday-trip conversation

scenario.gentle: Bea walked back through the conversation about the Saturday trip later that night, after her husband had gone to bed. It had started, she remembered, as a clean Adult-to-Adult exchange about whether they wanted to drive up to her sister's on Saturday. Somewhere in the middle her husband had said, 'You always do this.' She remembered the moment her own voice had changed, and the moment she had stopped wanting to talk about the trip and started wanting to win the conversation about whether she 'always' did anything. Tracing the seam, she could see exactly where the second arrow had stopped lining up with the first.
scenario.direct: Bea's narrative flashback: the Saturday-trip conversation, reconstructed three hours later. Opening exchange: Adult to Adult about driving to her sister's. Second exchange: husband sends 'You always do this' from his Parent, aimed at her Child. Bea answers from her own Parent, escalating. The original arrow was about a trip; the second arrow was about a long-running grievance. By the third exchange both of them were in different conversations.
scenario.competitive: Bea spent ninety minutes after her husband went to bed walking the conversation backwards looking for the seam. The opening had been clean: an Adult question about Saturday. The second move was 'you always do this,' which had been a Parent arrow into her Child. She remembered her own state changing in the next sentence and remembered that the next sentence had been the moment she stopped trying to plan a Saturday and started trying to win a fight she had not signed up for. The decision in front of her now was whether to bring the seam to her husband in the morning, or to let it go and run the same conversation again next month.

whatToDo.gentle: When you find the seam of a routine conversation that fell apart, the next move is rarely to relitigate the whole conversation. It is to bring the seam itself to the other person, briefly, and ask whether they want to start at the seam tomorrow. 'Last night, around the part where you said I always do this, I think the conversation changed shape. Can we go back to there?'
whatToDo.direct: Bring the seam, not the fight. 'I noticed the conversation last night changed shape around the moment you said I always do this. Can we restart from there?' The sentence is short on purpose. Long versions reopen the full disagreement; short versions name the structural moment and ask for a recross.
whatToDo.competitive: Walk in with the seam, not the grievance. One sentence: 'Last night, around the part where you said I always do this, the conversation changed shape. Can we restart there?' Anything longer is the next instance of the same fight. The seam-naming is the only move that is not the fight.

whyItMatters.gentle: Routine conversations between long-term partners that fall apart are usually crossed in a specific sentence. Couples who can name the sentence have a different fight available the next time. Couples who cannot are running the same fight in slightly different rooms.
whyItMatters.direct: Long-term relationships accumulate routine crossed transactions that recur because the cross point is never named. Naming it converts a recurring fight into a structural question, and structural questions can sometimes actually be answered.
whyItMatters.competitive: Couples who can locate the seam after the fact have a different fight available the next time. Couples who cannot are running the same fight in slightly different rooms for years, paying for it on Saturdays they keep not taking.

questions.prompt: In Berne's notation, when does a transaction count as complementary?
choices: When both people in the conversation are calm
When the response addresses the same topic as the stimulus
When the response comes from the state the stimulus addressed and is aimed back at the state the stimulus came from

explanation.gentle: Complementary is a structural fact about which states the two arrows connect. It is not about calmness, and it is not about staying on topic. Two people can be perfectly calm and still be in a crossed transaction; two people can be on the same topic and still be crossed.
explanation.direct: Complementary is defined by the alignment of the two arrows: the response coming from the addressed state and aiming back at the sender state. Calmness is a tone, not an alignment. Topic continuity is content, not structure.
explanation.competitive: Alignment of the arrows is the diagnosis. Tone is irrelevant; the chapter says crossed transactions can be perfectly polite. Topic is irrelevant; people can stay on topic and still cross.

questions.prompt: In the Tuesday stand-up where Tomas asks Aiya whether the API change will land Friday, what is the marker that the second exchange has crossed the first?
choices: Aiya answers from Parent in a tone that addresses Tomas as a Child who has not been listening, and Tomas's face changes before he can decide what to do with it
Aiya answers slowly
Tomas asks the question twice

explanation.gentle: The marker is structural and visible: the response came from a different state than the question, and aimed back at a different state too. Tomas's face changing is the body's signal that the second arrow did not land where the first one was waiting. Slow answers and repeated questions are not the marker; they are downstream consequences.
explanation.direct: State mismatch in the second arrow is the marker. The body's reaction is the early signal because state changes register faster than vocabulary. Slowness and repetition are not the marker; they are noise that sometimes accompanies a cross.
explanation.competitive: Mismatch of states in the second arrow is what you are looking for. Tomas's involuntary face change is the body acknowledging the cross before vocabulary can. Slow answers and repetition are not diagnostic of anything in particular.

questions.prompt: A team lead says, 'Can someone post the deploy log before the retro?' A junior engineer replies, 'Sorry, I'll do it.' Which kind of transaction is this most likely to be?
choices: Complementary, Adult to Adult
Crossed, with the lead's Adult addressed and the engineer answering from Adapted Child
Ulterior

explanation.gentle: The 'sorry' is the marker. Nothing in the lead's question called for an apology; the question was an Adult-to-Adult request for an action. The 'sorry' inserts an Adapted Child where the lead had aimed at Adult, which is exactly the structure of a cross. Ulterior is a different chapter.
explanation.direct: An Adult request answered by an apology is a small but textbook cross: the response comes from Adapted Child instead of Adult. Calling it complementary misreads the apology as content. Calling it ulterior crosses into territory the chapter has not covered yet.
explanation.competitive: Apology to an Adult action request is the cross. Reading it as complementary misses what the 'sorry' is doing structurally. Reading it as ulterior is jumping a chapter ahead, into material that has not been introduced.

questions.prompt: Coach Reyes and Diego have run the same Nurturing-Parent-to-Adapted-Child exchange after every bad race for two seasons. According to the chapter, what is the most accurate description of this exchange?
choices: Crossed, because Reyes is using the wrong tone
An ulterior transaction, because Reyes wants something underneath
Complementary and stable, and exactly the conversation that has prevented the conversation Diego actually needs

explanation.gentle: The exchange is fully complementary. Both arrows line up. Stable does not mean good, and the chapter is careful about that distinction. The trap is the moral reading that complementary exchanges are valuable just because they last; sometimes they last because they are crowding out the conversation that would matter.
explanation.direct: Complementary, stable, and crowding out a needed conversation is the chapter's point about Reyes and Diego. Calling it crossed misreads the alignment. Calling it ulterior is another chapter's vocabulary.
explanation.competitive: Stable on the wrong vector is the diagnosis. Calling it crossed gets the alignment wrong. Calling it ulterior borrows vocabulary the chapter has explicitly left for later.

questions.prompt: Yusuf is in his thesis advisor Mara's office. She asks an Adult question about a paragraph. He hears himself answer, 'I'm sorry, I know it's not working.' What has just happened, in the chapter's terms?
choices: Yusuf has crossed his own transaction by constructing a Parent in Mara that she had not been in, and answering it from Adapted Child
Mara has crossed the transaction by being secretly disappointed
The transaction is complementary because both people are trying to fix the chapter

explanation.gentle: This is a self-crossed transaction. Yusuf built a Parent role for Mara that she was not actually in, and then answered to it. The chapter calls these the hardest crosses to spot because the Parent you are answering is one you constructed. Treating it as Mara's cross misses where the construction happened. Treating it as complementary substitutes intention for structure.
explanation.direct: Self-crossed transactions are real and the chapter names them. Yusuf invented a Parent and answered it. Saying Mara crossed it locates the cross in the wrong person. Calling it complementary mistakes intention for state alignment.
explanation.competitive: Yusuf invented the Parent, then answered it. The cross is on his side of the table, not Mara's. Locating it on Mara is the misread the chapter is built to refuse. Calling it complementary mistakes shared good intention for arrow alignment.

questions.prompt: Olivia calls her sister Kenji from her Child asking for comfort, and Kenji answers from Adult with 'What specifically happened on Tuesday?' The chapter says both sisters are technically right. What does the chapter mean by that?
choices: Both answers are equally helpful
Each sister sent a coherent message from a coherent state, and the cross is structural rather than anyone's failure of intent or character
The transaction is actually complementary because both sisters care

explanation.gentle: The chapter is being careful with the word 'right.' It is not saying both answers were equally useful, and it is not saying nobody is to blame because both people care. It is saying the cross is structural: each sister sent a coherent arrow from a coherent state, and the arrows did not line up, and that is the whole story.
explanation.direct: Structural mismatch, not moral failure, is what 'technically right' is doing. Saying the answers were equally helpful collapses the chapter's distinction between alignment and value. Saying it was complementary because they care confuses intent with structure.
explanation.competitive: 'Technically right' marks the chapter's refusal to assign blame. Each sister sent a coherent arrow. The arrows did not align. That is the diagnosis, and it is silent on whether either of them was being a good sister.

questions.prompt: A customer phones a help line and asks, 'How do I cancel my subscription?' The agent replies, 'I'm sorry to hear you're considering leaving. Can you tell me more about what's not working for you?' Which kind of transaction is this most likely to be?
choices: Complementary, Adult to Adult
Complementary, Parent to Child
Crossed: an Adult information request answered by a Nurturing Parent that aims at the customer's Child

explanation.gentle: The customer asked an Adult question with one answer in it: a procedure for cancellation. The agent's response sounds caring but does the structural work of treating the customer as someone whose feelings should be processed before their request is honored. That is a Nurturing Parent move aimed at Child, and it crosses the original arrow.
explanation.direct: Information request answered by a feelings inquiry is the cross. The Nurturing-Parent face is what makes it look like service; the structure is still misaligned. Calling either of the complementary options correct misses the state mismatch.

chapters.title: Ulterior Transactions and the Anatomy of a Game

chapterBreakdown.gentle: You already know the dinner party where somebody asks for advice about a problem and then, one by one, explains why every suggestion will not work. On the surface, it looks like asking for help. Underneath, something else is running. Berne said that some transactions have two levels at once. The top level has the words in it. The bottom level has the pattern in it, and the pattern is usually the conversation that actually matters. When a two-level exchange repeats between the same people, with the same shape, and pays off in the same way each time, Berne called it a game. It is not playful. It is a reliable way to get a kind of attention both people need, at the cost of the conversation they would otherwise be having. The chapter names what makes it a game and why that naming matters to the reader who recognizes it.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Some transactions run on two levels at once. On the social level, the level in which words are exchanged, one thing is happening. On the psychological level, the level in which patterns are exchanged, something else is happening, and the second level is the one that actually matters. Berne called these ulterior transactions. He then proposed that when an ulterior transaction repeats between the same people, with the same opening move, the same counter, the same switch, and the same predictable outcome, it has become a game in his technical sense. A game has four structural parts you can name: thesis (the repeating plot), antithesis (the move that would break it), dynamics (the mechanism that keeps it running), and payoff (what both players get out of losing). The four parts let you see the game as a structure, not as a character flaw in either player. That is what makes the model useful rather than just accusatory.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: In any relationship where the same painful conversation keeps happening with the same shape, you are not in a series of accidents. You are in a pattern that is paying off for both people, at the cost of something neither of them is admitting. Berne built the vocabulary for this. Some transactions run on two levels at once: a social level that has words in it, and a psychological level that has the pattern in it. When the pattern repeats, it is a game in his technical sense, and every game has a shape you can name in four parts. Thesis, antithesis, dynamics, payoff. Learning to see the shape in real time is the leverage. Choosing whether to break the shape is a harder, more expensive decision that the diagnosis does not make for you. But the diagnosis is the prerequisite. You cannot make the choice without it.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Once you can draw the two arrows of a single transaction, the next thing the model gives you is a way to see what is running underneath them. Berne noticed that some transactions have two levels at the same time. On the top level, the level that has words in it, one conversation is happening. On the bottom level, the level that has no words but has a pattern in it, a different conversation is happening. The second conversation is usually the one that actually matters.

The clearest example is the dinner party where Lena asks for advice about her commute and rejects every suggestion with 'yes, but.' On the top level, Lena is asking for help. Underneath, she is demonstrating that nobody can help her, and the guests are obligingly generating fresh suggestions for her to reject. Berne called two-level transactions ulterior. He then took one more step. When an ulterior transaction runs repeatedly between the same people, with the same opening move, the same predictable counter, the same switch at the moment the psychological level takes over, and the same predictable payoff, it has become what he called a game.

The word is doing specific work. A game in Berne's technical usage is not playful. It is not what people mean in the loose sense when they say somebody is 'playing games.' It is a structural object with four nameable parts. The thesis is the repeating plot. The antithesis is the move that would break the game by refusing the role it has assigned. The dynamics are the mechanism that keeps it running. The payoff is what both players get out of the losing position, which is always more than it looks like from the outside, and always less than what the loss costs them.

The game has a shape both players recognize before the opening move is made. The shape is not the problem. The problem is that the shape is cheaper than the conversation it is replacing, and both players know it, and neither one has figured out what to do instead. That is the chapter's claim about why games persist: they are solutions, not accidents.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne's third structural move, after the three states and the two-arrow transaction, was to introduce the second level that runs underneath some transactions. He called it the ulterior level. On the social level, words are exchanged; on the psychological level, patterns are exchanged, and the psychological level is where the actual work of the conversation is being done. Lena at a dinner party asks her guests for advice about her commute and rejects every suggestion with 'yes, but.' The social level is a request for help. The ulterior level is a demonstration that nobody can help her, and the guests, by generating new suggestions for her to reject, are participating in the demonstration without noticing.

Berne then defined a game as an ongoing series of ulterior transactions that progress reliably toward a predictable outcome. The word 'game' is doing specific work. It does not mean playful. It does not mean the loose thing people point at when they say a friend is 'playing games' with them. It means a structural object with a repeating shape and a predictable payoff. Every game has four nameable parts.

Thesis is the repeating plot: an opening move, a predictable counter, a switch at the moment the psychological level takes over, and a payoff. Antithesis is the move that would break the game by refusing the role it has assigned one of the players. Dynamics is the psychological mechanism that keeps the game running. Payoff is what both players get out of the losing position, which is usually a reliable source of attention (what Berne called strokes, a word that belongs properly to the next chapter) plus a confirmation of a position about themselves or the world that they were already holding. The game is not an accident. It is a solution to a problem the player has not solved any other way.

This is why the diagnosis has to be held carefully. The reader who names the game without understanding what it is solving will try to remove the game before the player has a replacement. Removing the solution before the problem has been addressed produces a worse outcome than the game, not a better one.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The reason the same painful conversation keeps happening in a relationship is almost never that the people in it are stupid. It is that the conversation is running on two levels at once, and the second level is paying them both something the first level cannot admit. Berne built the vocabulary for that.

On the top level, the level with words in it, one exchange is happening. On the bottom level, the level with the pattern in it, something else is. Lena at the dinner party asks for advice and rejects every suggestion. On the top level, she is asking for help. On the bottom level, she is proving that no one can help her, and her guests are proving it with her every time they offer another suggestion. Berne called the bottom level ulterior, and he named something harder: when an ulterior transaction repeats between the same people with the same shape, it is a game in his technical sense, and every game is a structural object with four nameable parts.

Thesis is the repeating plot: opening move, counter, switch, payoff. Antithesis is the move that would break the game by refusing the role it assigned. Dynamics is the mechanism that keeps the whole thing in motion. Payoff is what both players get from the losing position, and it is always something real, even when it is a kind of attention the player would rather not admit they needed. A game is not a metaphor. It is a solution the player has found to a problem they have not solved any other way, and that is why shaming it does not work. The leverage, as always, is in the reading, not in the shaming. Reading the second level before the game has finished its next round is the cheapest intervention available, and the easiest one to misuse.

Using the anatomy to shame the player or demand the antithesis before the player has a replacement supply of strokes is the standard misuse. The model was built to locate games, not to accelerate exits from games the player cannot yet afford to leave. That limit belongs in the same sentence as the diagnosis, not in a footnote.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The three voices alone were observation. The two arrows of a transaction were a relational tool. The model's third move, the one Berne took in his most important chapter, was to add the second level that runs underneath some transactions. Some exchanges are two-layer. On the top layer, the layer that has words in it, one kind of conversation is happening. On the bottom layer, the layer that has the pattern in it, a different kind of conversation is happening. The second one is usually the one that actually matters.

The clearest worked example is small and social. Lena asks her dinner party for advice about her morning commute and rejects every suggestion the guests offer with 'yes, but.' On the top level, Lena is asking for help. Underneath, she is demonstrating that nobody at the table can help her, and the guests are participating in the demonstration by generating fresh suggestions for her to reject. The surface conversation is about the commute. The actual conversation is about Lena's position in the world (unhelpable, interestingly hard) and the guests' position (concerned friends who tried). Berne called the second level ulterior, and that word is the whole first half of the chapter.

The second half is the harder move. Berne noticed that when an ulterior transaction repeats between the same people, with the same opening move, the same predictable counter, the same switch at the moment the psychological level takes over, and the same reliable payoff, it stops being a one-off and becomes what he called a game. A game in his technical usage is not playful, and it is not the loose thing people mean when they say somebody is 'playing games' with them. It is a structural object with four nameable parts. Thesis is the repeating plot. Antithesis is the move that would break the game by refusing the role it has assigned. Dynamics is the mechanism that keeps the pattern running. Payoff is what both players get out of the losing position, which is usually a reliable kind of attention plus a confirmation of something they already believe about themselves or about the world.

Two things have to live next to each other in the rest of the chapter, and they cut against each other on purpose. The first is that the anatomy is real. You can name the four parts of a game someone in your life is running, and you can often name the antithesis that would break it. The second is that the antithesis is expensive, in ways the anatomy alone does not show you. Naming the game will come next.

But naming is not the whole work, and the chapter is careful about that. The anatomy describes what is happening. It does not automatically point to whether the game should be broken, or who should break it, or what would need to be in place before breaking it was survivable for the player running it. Those questions require more than a clear diagnosis. They require the reader to hold both the clarity of the anatomy and the weight of what the game has been providing before deciding what, if anything, to do with either.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne's third structural move after the three states and the two-arrow transaction was to introduce the second level that runs underneath some transactions. He called it the ulterior level. On the social level of a transaction, words are exchanged. On the ulterior level, patterns are exchanged, and the ulterior level is where the actual work of the conversation is being done. When Lena at a dinner party asks her guests for advice about her commute and rejects every suggestion with 'yes, but,' the social level is a request for help and the ulterior level is a demonstration that nobody can help her. Both levels are running at the same time. Both levels are part of the same transaction. The guests are participating in the ulterior level without having been told about it.

Berne then took the second, harder step. He proposed that when an ulterior transaction runs repeatedly between the same people, with the same opening move, the same predictable counter, the same switch at the moment the psychological level takes over, and the same reliable payoff, it has become what he technically called a game. The word 'game' is doing specific work here. It does not mean playful, and it does not mean the loose thing people point at when they say somebody is playing games with them. It means a structural object with a repeating shape and a predictable outcome.

Every game has four nameable structural features, and Berne is strict about them. The thesis is the repeating plot: opening move, counter, switch, payoff, in a sequence the participants could describe if they were pushed hard enough. The antithesis is the specific move that would break the game by refusing the role it has assigned to one of the players, and the antithesis is almost always uncomfortable because it requires ignoring the social level and responding to the ulterior level directly. The dynamics are the psychological mechanism that keeps the whole pattern in motion, and the dynamics are usually about something the player needs and does not have a better source for. The payoff is what the player gets out of the losing position, which is always more than it looks like from outside and always less than what the loss is costing them.

Two structural facts must travel together into the hard-depth version of this chapter. The first is that the anatomy is real and operational. You can apply it to recurring painful patterns in your own life and get a clear diagnosis. The second is that applying it to other people's games, or using it to demand the antithesis from someone who has nowhere else to go for what the game provides, is one of the fastest ways to make the model harmful. The next section holds that limit.

The anatomy is a precision tool. Its accuracy does not make it safe to apply at full force against every game a reader can now identify. The cases where the model becomes harmful are the ones where the reader knows the antithesis, knows they could execute it, and does so without asking what the game was providing for the person running it. A sharp diagnosis deployed without that question is still a diagnosis; it is also a kind of ambush.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Pay attention to what the chapter is actually claiming, because the word 'game' in Berne's technical usage is easy to misread and the misread makes the rest of the book sound cynical. He is not saying that people are playing games with each other in the loose sense that word has in English, and he is not being contemptuous of people who play games. He is proposing a structural claim: some transactions run on two levels at once, and when the two-level structure repeats between the same people with the same shape and pays off in the same way every time, the pattern has become an object with four nameable parts.

The first half of the claim is about the transaction. On the social level of an exchange, words are exchanged. On the ulterior level, underneath, a pattern is exchanged. Lena at a dinner party asks for advice about her commute and rejects every suggestion. On the social level she is asking for help. On the ulterior level she is demonstrating that nobody can help her, and the guests are generating her demonstrations for her by continuing to make suggestions she can reject. Neither side is doing this on purpose. The ulterior level is just as real as the social level, and the two are running at the same time.

The second half of the claim is about the repetition. A single ulterior transaction is not yet a game. A game is what you have when the same ulterior transaction repeats between the same people with a recognizable shape: an opening move, a predictable counter, a switch at the moment the psychological level takes over, and a payoff that both players get something from. The thesis is the repeating plot. The antithesis is the move that would break the game by refusing the role it assigned. The dynamics are the mechanism that keeps the whole pattern running. The payoff is what the player gets out of losing, which is almost always a reliable kind of attention plus a confirmation of something they already believed about themselves or the world.

The leverage in the chapter, and the reason it has to come before chapter four and not after, is that the anatomy gives the reader a real diagnostic tool. The cost the chapter cannot skip is that the tool is expensive to swing. Applying it to your own games is useful. Applying it to other people's games, or using it to demand the antithesis from someone who has nowhere else to go for what the game is providing, is how a reader weaponizes the model against the people they should be most careful with. The next section is where the chapter pays for that distinction honestly.

The reader who can name every game in the room but cannot resist naming it aloud has turned the model into a weapon, and the weapon's first casualty is the relationship the model was supposed to help them read. Precision without restraint is not sophistication. The chapter asks for both, and makes the case that the restraint is the harder skill of the two to acquire once the anatomy is in the reader's hands.

activationPrompt.gentle: Think about a recurring pattern in a close relationship you have been running for years. Try to name all four parts: the repeating plot, the move that would break it, the mechanism that keeps it going, and what both of you get out of it.
activationPrompt.direct: Identify a recurring game in a long-term relationship of yours. Name the thesis, antithesis, dynamics, and payoff in specific terms, including what the payoff is actually paying you.
activationPrompt.competitive: Pick the longest-running recurring pattern in any relationship you are in. Write out the four structural features in concrete sentences, with specific payoffs. If you cannot name the payoff, you do not yet see the game.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: When did you most recently catch yourself participating in an ulterior transaction from the side of the generator, the guest at the dinner party offering suggestions that kept being rejected?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Name the last time you were the one offering advice that kept being rejected. What was the ulterior level, and how long did it take you to notice?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Find the most recent time you were cast as the advice-generator in someone else's rejected-suggestion game. How many suggestions did you offer before you saw it? If more than three, you were not yet reading the second level.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: Where in your life is there a stable, recurring game that you are the player of, and what would the antithesis cost you if you tried to break it?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Identify a stable game of your own. Name its payoff specifically. Then describe what you would lose if you broke it tomorrow, in concrete terms.
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Name one game you run on yourself. Describe the payoff with enough specificity that you can see why shaming yourself will not make it go away. The specific payoff is what you would need a replacement for.
