scenario.gentle: It is Tuesday again. Victor's retrospective. I am on the call with my coffee in the cup I bought the day I joined this team. Victor opens with the same sentence he has opened with for eight months: 'Does anyone have anything they want to raise?' I watch the three-second silence arrive, right on schedule. I used to break the silence. I do not anymore, because I remember what happened the last three times I did. Victor says, 'Great, no issues this week.' I do not drink the coffee. The meeting ends, and I am noticing, for the first time today, that I already know the whole shape of the thing we are all in.
scenario.direct: Tuesday standing retrospective. POV: Teodora, eight months on the team. Victor (team lead) opens with 'Does anyone have anything they want to raise?' The three-second silence that follows is scripted now. I used to speak into it. The last three times I did, Victor responded in ways that were technically polite and practically punishing. Now I sit. The meeting closes with 'no issues this week.' The reporting upward is clean. I am watching myself participate in a pattern I did not sign up for and have no obvious way to leave.
scenario.competitive: Tuesday retro, month eight. Victor's opening line never changes: 'Does anyone have anything they want to raise?' Mine never changes either anymore: silence, the coffee cup I keep in my hand so my hands have a job. The first three times I raised something in this meeting, Victor's half-second pause taught me what this room was going to cost me. Now I do not pay. I also do not have the meeting I came to have. The pattern is paying Victor's reporting cleaner numbers every week, and it is paying me a quieter hour in exchange for my voice. That is the deal, and nobody in the room voted on it.

whatToDo.gentle: When you catch yourself inside a group-level game, the first move is not necessarily to break it. It is to name it to yourself clearly, including your own participation, and to decide whether this is a meeting you can raise a thing in or a meeting you need to raise the thing outside of. Often the correct first move is the offline conversation with someone outside the meeting.
whatToDo.direct: Take the topic you would have raised in the retro to a channel the retro does not cover. Write it up, one paragraph, and send it to Victor's manager, or to a peer lead, or to whoever owns the thing. The retro is a closed system; raising it inside the retro is playing the game. Raising it outside the retro is the antithesis.
whatToDo.competitive: Stop raising it in the room the game owns. Take the topic to the channel above the retro, in writing, with dates. The retro exists to absorb feedback; the written escalation exists outside the retro's ulterior level. One written escalation will teach Victor more about what the room is for than twelve broken silences.

whyItMatters.gentle: Group-level games eat more of your working life than one-on-one games because they run on a schedule. Catching the pattern once is not the same as leaving the pattern; leaving it requires finding a channel the game does not own.
whyItMatters.direct: Group games are structural because the meeting itself is structural. The antithesis for a group game is usually to move the message out of the meeting, not to break the meeting. Breaking the meeting almost always costs the breaker more than the meeting is worth.
whyItMatters.competitive: Group games are the most expensive pattern a professional ever enters, because they run weekly and the payoff is paid in organizational attention the player cannot route around. The only cheap exit is out of the meeting itself, in writing, to somebody the meeting does not own.

scenario.gentle: Petra, Teodora's manager, calls her into the glass-walled office on Thursday afternoon for what Petra's calendar calls a 'quick 1:1.' Petra opens with, 'I wanted to see if there was anything I could help with on the migration. Can I help you re-scope it?' On the social level, it is an offer of support. Teodora hears it and feels her stomach do a small familiar thing, because she has taken this offer before and remembers how it ended: a re-scope that quietly made her look like the person who had been over-promising.
scenario.direct: Thursday afternoon, Petra's glass-walled office. Petra (Adult to Adult, on the social level): I wanted to see if there was anything I could help with on the migration. Can I help you re-scope it? On the ulterior level: the offer is a setup. The last two 're-scopes' made Teodora look like the person who had been over-committing. Teodora is reading both levels at once and trying to decide which one to answer.
scenario.competitive: Petra asked the question with a calendar invite that said 'quick 1:1.' On the top level it was an offer of help. On the bottom level it was the move that turned Teodora's previous project into Teodora's over-promise. Teodora knew both levels, watched Petra's face arrange itself into the helpful expression, and understood she had about ninety seconds to decide whether to answer the top level or the bottom level of the question.

whatToDo.gentle: When you recognize an ulterior offer, do not refuse the help outright. That triggers the social-level story that you are being difficult. Instead, accept the help in a form that breaks the ulterior level. 'I'd love your help. Can you send me a written list of what you think the right scope is, and we can compare it to mine?' The written list is the antithesis.
whatToDo.direct: Accept the help in writing only. 'Yes, please send me your proposed re-scope in writing and I will compare it to mine.' The request for a written artifact interrupts the ulterior level because the ulterior level runs on plausible deniability. A written document has no plausible deniability.
whatToDo.competitive: Convert the offer into a deliverable. 'Please send me your proposed re-scope in writing by end of day Friday, and I will compare it line by line to mine.' The written artifact is the move the ulterior level cannot survive, because the ulterior level depends on the help being vague enough to shift blame later.

whyItMatters.gentle: Most workplace ulterior offers rely on the help being informal enough to be deniable later. Turning the offer into a written artifact is not about blame; it is about keeping the record of what was actually offered.
whyItMatters.direct: Ulterior offers in the workplace live in the gap between what was said verbally and what gets documented later. Closing the gap with a written artifact is the cleanest antithesis available to a subordinate.
whyItMatters.competitive: The written artifact is the cheapest defense a subordinate has against a manager's ulterior offer, and it is one of the only defenses that also scales. Informal help is where the payoff of the manager's game lives. Formal help destroys the ulterior level without requiring a confrontation.

examples.title: Farida's dissertation proposal in Imani's seminar

scenario.gentle: In Professor Imani's Friday methods seminar, Farida has presented a draft of her dissertation proposal and asked for feedback. Imani suggested that Farida read a specific methodological critique. Farida said, 'Yes, but I've tried that author before and I don't connect with his framing.' Imani suggested a second author. Farida said, 'Yes, but that one is a little too quantitative for my question.' Imani suggested a third, and Farida began with 'yes, but.' Imani paused mid-sentence and reread something on her copy of the draft.
scenario.direct: IMANI (Adult to Adult): Try reading this methodological critique. FARIDA: Yes, but I don't connect with that author's framing. IMANI: Try this other author. FARIDA: Yes, but too quantitative. IMANI: Try this third author. FARIDA: Yes, but... Imani stops mid-sentence. The social level is feedback. The ulterior level is Farida demonstrating that no author can help her and Imani being set up to keep generating authors.
scenario.competitive: Farida presented her proposal in Imani's seminar and then rejected the first three suggestions with 'yes, but.' Imani was eight minutes into the session when she caught the shape of the conversation she was in. The social level was dissertation feedback. The ulterior level was a game Imani had seen other students play with other professors, and the payoff at the end was going to be Farida explaining, in her next committee meeting, that she had consulted Professor Imani and none of the suggestions had been workable. Imani had been set up as the witness to the impossibility. She stopped mid-sentence.

whatToDo.gentle: The professor's move here is not to keep suggesting authors. It is to hand the question back. 'Farida, I notice I have suggested three authors and none of them have been useful. I am going to stop suggesting. What is the author you would suggest for yourself?'
whatToDo.direct: Refuse to offer the fourth suggestion. Replace it with a question about what Farida has already tried, in her own words. 'What is the author you would recommend for yourself?' That question is the antithesis; it refuses the role of suggestion-generator and hands the problem back.
whatToDo.competitive: Cut the suggestions cold. 'I have offered three authors. I am done offering authors. Tell me which author you would recommend for yourself, and we will talk about that one.' The sentence is sharp on purpose. The sharpness is what the game cannot absorb.

whyItMatters.gentle: Rejected-suggestion patterns in advising relationships waste years of the advisor's time and quietly harm the student's thesis. Reframing the conversation, once, as 'what would you recommend' is often enough to either break the pattern or reveal that the student needs a different kind of conversation entirely.
whyItMatters.direct: Rejected-suggestion patterns are a common game in academic advising. Reframing from 'here is a suggestion' to 'what would you suggest' converts a generator role into a consultant role, which the game cannot run on.
whyItMatters.competitive: An advisor who keeps generating suggestions for a student who runs a rejected-suggestion game is losing hours of their own research time every week and providing the student with the raw material for a future complaint about not being supported. The reframe is the only cheap exit, and it has to happen the moment the advisor notices the pattern.

examples.title: Hana coaches Wole after the parent meeting

scenario.gentle: Hana is sitting in the teachers' lounge after the last bell with her colleague Wole, who is two years into the job and has just had a hard conversation with a student's parents. Wole is describing the meeting. 'Every time I asked them about the homework, they said they were trying their best. I just kept asking different ways.' Hana recognizes the shape Wole is describing from the other side. She wants to name it for him without calling it a game out loud, because the word 'game' will sound cynical to Wole, and cynical is not what this is.
scenario.direct: Teachers' lounge after last bell. Wole (2 years into teaching, Adult to Adult): Every time I asked them about the homework, they said they were trying their best. I kept asking different ways. Hana (Adult, coaching register): You kept asking different ways because nothing you asked got you closer to what you actually wanted to know. That is the signal. The conversation had two levels and you were only being allowed to work the top one.
scenario.competitive: Wole was describing a parent meeting in the teachers' lounge and Hana was recognizing the game at speed. Every rephrased question the parents answered with 'we are doing our best' was a move in a pattern Hana had seen a dozen times. The social level was a parent conference. The ulterior level was the parents declining, politely, to be in any conversation that could produce an actionable next step. Hana's problem was how to hand Wole the diagnosis without using the word 'game,' which was going to sound wrong in his ear on his second year of teaching.

whatToDo.gentle: Instead of saying 'they were playing a game,' say 'there were two conversations in the room and you were only invited to work on one of them.' That sentence lands with a teacher like Wole because it is true on both the social and structural level without asking him to be cynical. Then ask him what the second conversation might have been, and let him answer in his own words.
whatToDo.direct: Describe the ulterior layer without the word 'game.' 'There was a second conversation in the room and you were not invited into it. What do you think the parents were protecting by saying they were doing their best?' That question hands the diagnosis to Wole without the language that will scare him off.
whatToDo.competitive: Do not use the word 'game.' Use the phrase 'second conversation' and hand Wole the diagnosis. 'The parents were having a second conversation in that meeting and you were not in it. What do you think they were protecting?' The sentence is the whole lesson, and it survives Wole's first reaction, which the word 'game' would not have.

whyItMatters.gentle: Teaching the second layer of the model to colleagues who are not steeped in Berne's vocabulary is the harder half of the skill. The phrase 'second conversation' is the most reliable bridge because it is literal, not cynical.
whyItMatters.direct: The word 'game' in Berne's sense does not survive translation into a lunchroom conversation with a colleague who has not read the book. Translating the diagnosis into 'second conversation' preserves the structure and loses the cynicism.
whyItMatters.competitive: Mid-career teachers who have been taught Berne's game vocabulary by a cynical colleague will refuse the model for the rest of their careers. The phrase 'second conversation,' handed at the right moment in a lounge conversation, is the only version of the model that survives first contact with a principled young teacher.

scenario.gentle: It is eleven at night, after the dinner party. Lena is standing at the kitchen island with the leftover plates and her phone face-down. She is thinking about the conversation about her commute, and about the three guests who offered suggestions, and about the word 'but' coming out of her mouth three times in a row. She is thinking about her guest Marcelo, who had said, at the end, in a gentle voice, 'What have you already tried?' and about how that question had made her angry in a way the other suggestions had not. She is recognizing something she does not yet have a word for, and she is not sure she wants to find the word tonight.
scenario.direct: 11 PM, after the dinner party. Kitchen island, leftover plates, phone face-down. Inner monologue: Lena reconstructs the 'yes, but' sequence with her three guests, and lands on the detail that Marcelo's 'what have you already tried' was the one question that made her angry. She recognizes, in real time, that the conversation had two levels and that she was running the second one. The recognition is uncomfortable. She is sitting with it because the alternative is pretending she is not.
scenario.competitive: 11 PM. The plates are on the counter and Lena's phone is face-down because she does not want to look at any messages from her guests yet. She is running the conversation back through her head and noticing, with more clarity than she wanted, that Marcelo's question 'what have you already tried' had made her angrier than any of the suggestions. The anger is the tell. The only reason that question would make her angry is that it refused the conversation she was actually running, and the only reason she would have been running that conversation is that she needed something out of it. She does not yet know what the something is. She is also not going to sleep until she has at least named it to herself.

whatToDo.gentle: The first move after noticing you are running a game on yourself is not to fix it. It is to write down what you noticed, as specifically as you can, without judgment. 'Tonight I rejected three suggestions. I got angry at Marcelo's question because it refused the conversation I was running. I do not yet know what I was running it for.' That note is the antithesis in its softest form: an honest record, with no decision attached.
whatToDo.direct: Write one sentence about what you noticed. 'I ran a rejected-suggestion pattern at dinner tonight and got angry at the one guest who refused to play.' Do not decide what to do about it yet. The record is the intervention.
whatToDo.competitive: Write it down before you go to bed. One sentence, no softening. 'I ran a rejected-suggestion game at dinner tonight and got angry at the only guest who refused to play.' The sentence has to survive you reading it in the morning. It has to be honest enough that you cannot explain it away.

whyItMatters.gentle: Recognizing a game you are running on yourself is the hardest kind of recognition because there is no one else to blame. It is also the only kind that gives you any leverage over the pattern. The note is the leverage.
whyItMatters.direct: Self-recognition of a game is the most valuable and the most painful form of the skill. The one-sentence written record is the minimum viable intervention and the maximum useful one in the short term.
whyItMatters.competitive: A player who can write down, honestly, the game they ran that evening has a different next month available. A player who cannot has the same next month they had the last twelve months. The sentence is the whole move.

scenario.gentle: Priscilla was standing at her son Nils's kitchen counter looking at the cabinet pulls he had bought and thinking about whether to say something about them. Then, without meaning to, she remembered her own mother standing at a kitchen counter in 1984, holding a phone to her ear, offering to help Priscilla plan her first apartment in a tone that Priscilla had never quite been able to describe. Her mother's Tupperware had been on the counter. The offer of help had sounded like love and had felt like something else. And Priscilla, at Nils's kitchen counter thirty-nine years later, recognized, in the sudden unpleasant way you recognize a face you meant never to see again, that she was about to say something about the cabinet pulls.
scenario.direct: Priscilla's narrative flashback, at her son Nils's kitchen remodel. She was about to comment on his cabinet pulls. She remembered, mid-breath, her own mother in 1984, offering to help her plan her first apartment in a tone that made 'help' a different word. Priscilla recognized, in real time, that the game she was about to play with Nils was the one her mother had played with her, and that the comment about the cabinet pulls would be the opening move. She is now at a decision point: make the comment or not.
scenario.competitive: She had the comment about the cabinet pulls fully formed in her mouth when she remembered her mother's Tupperware on the counter in 1984. That was the sentence that had taught her what kind of help to expect. Her mother had played this exact game with her, using cabinet pulls or curtain rods or paint colors as the opening move, for thirty-nine years. Priscilla had sworn she would never run it on Nils. She was about to run it on Nils. She had about three seconds to decide whether that was a pattern she was going to continue paying for or end in the next sentence.

whatToDo.gentle: When you recognize yourself about to make the opening move of a game you inherited, the move is not to give a speech. It is to close your mouth on the opening sentence and replace it with something that does not have the game in it. 'The kitchen looks beautiful, Nils. I am going to go sit down.' That sentence is short on purpose. Short is how inherited games get interrupted.
whatToDo.direct: Close your mouth on the opening move. Replace it with the shortest kind sentence you can form that does not contain a suggestion or a correction. 'The kitchen looks beautiful. I am going to sit down.' Short because the game lives in elaboration.
whatToDo.competitive: Do not finish the sentence. Whatever else you say, it cannot start with the cabinet pulls. 'The kitchen looks beautiful. I am going to sit down.' Fifteen words. The game cannot live in fifteen words. Anything longer gives it room.

whyItMatters.gentle: Inherited games are the hardest to interrupt because the opening move feels like being yourself. Interrupting one, even once, is a real structural change, and it is usually the first time a generational pattern has been broken in the relationship.
whyItMatters.direct: Multi-generational games pass through families as 'how we are' and get interrupted, when they get interrupted at all, one opening move at a time. A single refused opening is a structural intervention.
whyItMatters.competitive: A parent who can refuse, even once, the opening move of the game their own parent played on them has changed the pattern that was going to run for another generation. The antithesis in that case is thirty-nine years overdue and costs exactly one sentence.

questions.prompt: In Berne's model, what makes a transaction ulterior?
choices: The two people in it are using tones that do not match their words
The transaction has two levels running at the same time, a social level in the words and a psychological level in the pattern underneath
The two people in it are secretly manipulating each other

explanation.gentle: Ulterior is a structural fact about two levels running at the same time, not a claim about tone and not a claim about conscious manipulation. People can be sincere in their words and still be in an ulterior transaction, and the two levels are both real regardless of whether either player notices them.
explanation.direct: Two levels running at once is the definition. Tone mismatch is a symptom, not the structure. Conscious manipulation is a strong overread; most ulterior transactions run without either player noticing them.
explanation.competitive: Two levels, running together. Tone mismatch is a hint, not the thing itself. Calling it manipulation is the cynical misread the chapter is built to refuse, and it makes the model unusable on your own patterns.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between an ulterior transaction and a game in Berne's sense?
choices: There is no difference; they are two names for the same thing
An ulterior transaction is conscious, and a game is unconscious
An ulterior transaction is a single two-level exchange; a game is what you have when the same ulterior transaction repeats between the same people with a recognizable shape and a predictable payoff

explanation.gentle: A single two-level exchange is not yet a game. A game is the object you have when the two-level exchange repeats with the same shape and pays off the same way every time. The chapter is strict about this distinction because conflating the two is how people start over-detecting games in other people's lives.
explanation.direct: Repetition with recognizable shape is what makes a game. A single ulterior transaction is not enough. Calling them identical collapses the chapter's core structural move; calling it a consciousness distinction gets the criterion wrong.
explanation.competitive: Repetition and predictable payoff are the criteria. Single ulterior transactions happen all the time and are not automatically games. Conflating them is how readers turn the chapter into a weapon against strangers.

questions.prompt: At Lena's dinner party, when she rejects every suggestion her guests offer with 'yes, but,' what is the most accurate description of the payoff the ulterior level is paying her?
choices: Reliable attention from her guests plus a confirmation that nobody can really help her, which is the position she was already holding
Actual solutions to her commute problem
Revenge against her guests for earlier slights

explanation.gentle: The chapter is careful here. The payoff is both a kind of attention (what Berne called strokes, a word that belongs to the next chapter) and a confirmation of Lena's existing position that the problem is insoluble. Actual solutions are what the social level claims to want; they are not what the ulterior level is paying. Revenge is a cynical misread.
explanation.direct: Attention plus position confirmation is the payoff. Solutions are what the social level asks for and the ulterior level is built to refuse. Revenge narratives overread the player and get the adaptive nature of the game wrong.
explanation.competitive: Attention and position confirmation. The game cannot pay out solutions because solutions would end the game, and Lena cannot afford for it to end until she has another source of what it is paying her. Revenge gets the motive wrong by making the player a villain instead of an adapter.

questions.prompt: In Victor's Tuesday retrospective, the three-second silence after his opening question 'Does anyone have anything they want to raise?' has become the moment everyone in the room waits through. Which structural feature of the game does the silence correspond to?
choices: The antithesis (the move that would break the game)
The dynamics (the mechanism that keeps the game running)
The switch inside the thesis (the moment the social-level story collapses into the psychological-level payoff)

explanation.gentle: The three-second silence is the moment the social-level invitation collapses into the psychological-level fact that the team has been trained not to raise anything. In Berne's notation that collapse moment is the switch inside the thesis. The antithesis would be somebody raising something in writing outside the meeting. The dynamics are the underlying mechanism, not the specific visible moment.
explanation.direct: Switch inside the thesis is the three-second silence. The silence is where the social story ('anyone have anything to raise?') gives way to the payoff ('no issues this week'). The antithesis is a move nobody has made yet. The dynamics are abstract and not visible as a specific moment.
explanation.competitive: Switch is the specific moment the top level collapses into the bottom one, and in Victor's retro that moment is the silence. Calling it the antithesis is confusing the problem with the fix. Calling it the dynamics mistakes the underlying machinery for its output.

questions.prompt: Petra calls Teodora into her office and asks, 'Can I help you re-scope the migration?' The chapter says this is an ulterior transaction. What are the two levels?
choices: Social level: an Adult-to-Adult offer of support. Psychological level: actually it is still just an Adult-to-Adult offer of support.
Social level: an offer of managerial help. Psychological level: a move that will later let Petra document Teodora as the person who over-committed, which is how the previous re-scope ended.
Social level: a Child-to-Parent appeal. Psychological level: a Parent-to-Child instruction.

explanation.gentle: The social level is an offer of help; the psychological level is the move that will let Petra document Teodora as the one who over-committed. The first wrong answer treats the transaction as single-layer, which the chapter is specifically trying to prevent. The second wrong answer confuses ulterior with a state-misalignment from the previous chapter.
explanation.direct: Two-level structure with help on top and a later-blame mechanism underneath is what makes it ulterior. Collapsing it to a single layer denies the chapter's point; describing it as Child/Parent misaligns concepts from the previous chapter with the concepts from this one.
explanation.competitive: Offer on top, setup underneath. Calling it single-layer throws away the chapter. Calling it a state mismatch from the previous chapter confuses vocabularies; ulterior is a two-level claim, not a state-alignment claim.

questions.prompt: In Priscilla's recurring pattern of helping her son Nils with his projects in a way that ensures each one fails, which mapping of the four-part anatomy is most accurate?
choices: Thesis: she offers, he accepts, she provides help that guarantees failure, she sighs. Antithesis: he declines or accepts on his own terms or names the pattern. Dynamics: her need to keep him in the position of needing her. Payoff: confirmation of the parent-child position.
Thesis: Nils is incompetent. Antithesis: Nils becomes competent. Dynamics: genetic predisposition. Payoff: Priscilla feels good.
Thesis: Priscilla is a bad mother. Antithesis: she stops being a bad mother. Dynamics: guilt. Payoff: none.

explanation.gentle: The chapter is specific about what each of the four parts is. The thesis is the repeating plot sequence. The antithesis is the move that refuses the assigned role. The dynamics are the psychological mechanism. The payoff is what both players get. The wrong answers either moralize the players, which the chapter refuses, or get the structural categories wrong.
explanation.direct: Correct mapping follows the chapter's strict usage. The incompetence-and-genetics answer fails because it assigns pathology to a person rather than structure to a pattern. The bad-mother answer fails because it moralizes, which is the failure mode the chapter is explicitly built to avoid.
explanation.competitive: Structural mapping, not character assassination. The wrong answers both swap the structural vocabulary for moral vocabulary, which is how the anatomy gets weaponized. The chapter exists in large part to prevent that swap.

questions.prompt: According to the chapter, what is the main risk of learning the four-part anatomy?
choices: The reader will become too cynical to enjoy dinner parties
The reader will break games without permission

The reader will start applying the anatomy to every painful interaction in their life, including ones that are not games (trauma, structural inequality, or simple mismatch of needs) and misdiagnose them

explanation.gentle: The chapter is explicit about the hammer problem: once the reader has the anatomy, they will be tempted to apply it universally, and not every hard conversation is a game. Some are grief, or power, or mismatch, and calling them games flattens them. Cynicism is a secondary risk; the deeper one is misdiagnosis.
explanation.direct: Over-detection is the central risk the chapter names. Cynicism is downstream; breaking-without-permission is a different failure and one the chapter treats under the antithesis-is-expensive limit. The hammer problem is the correct phrasing of the primary danger.
explanation.competitive: Over-detection, not cynicism or over-intervention, is the hammer problem. Every hard conversation is not a game, and the anatomy applied to grief or power becomes a weapon against the exact people the reader should be most careful with.

questions.prompt: Of the moves below, which one is the antithesis to Lena's dinner party game, and what does the chapter say it costs?
choices: Offering Lena a fourth, better suggestion; the cost is nothing because good suggestions always help

Asking Lena 'what have you already tried?' and refusing to generate a fourth suggestion; the cost is that Lena loses the payoff she was getting from the game and may get angry, because she has not yet found a better source of what the game was paying her
Leaving the dinner party; the cost is that Lena will complain about you to mutual friends

explanation.gentle: The antithesis is the question that refuses the role of suggestion-generator and hands the problem back to Lena. The cost is the payoff she was getting from the game, which is real even though it looks small. Offering a fourth suggestion is still playing; leaving is not the antithesis, it is exit.
explanation.direct: Refusing the generator role and asking what Lena has already tried is the antithesis. The fourth suggestion is another move inside the game, not a move that breaks it. Leaving is an escape, not an antithesis; the chapter distinguishes between them.
explanation.competitive: Refuse the role and hand the problem back. The fourth suggestion is still a move inside the game; leaving is exit, not antithesis. The cost of the real antithesis is the payoff Lena was getting from the game, and the chapter is honest that she may get angry because of it.

questions.prompt: The chapter insists that seeing a game is not the same as choosing to break it. What is the main reason?
choices: Because the antithesis is expensive: breaking the game takes away the payoff the player has been using, and if they do not have a better source of what the payoff was providing, naming the game can hurt before it helps
Because the other person has to give consent first
Because the reader is not qualified to diagnose games unless they are a therapist

explanation.gentle: The chapter's honest accounting is that the antithesis removes the payoff, and the payoff is always something the player needed. If they had a better source of it, they would already be using it. Consent is a different framing and not what the chapter says. The qualification answer turns the chapter into a professional-gatekeeping story, which it is not.
explanation.direct: Expense of the antithesis is the chapter's argument. The consent framing misreads the chapter; the qualification framing replaces the chapter's structural argument with a credentialing one.
explanation.competitive: Cost. That is the whole argument. The consent framing substitutes a different model's vocabulary, and the credentialing framing turns a tool the chapter gives to any reader into a gated one, which the chapter explicitly refuses.

questions.prompt: Combining the three chapters so far, what can a reader do with all three tools that they could not do with any single chapter's tool alone?
choices: Pick the best ego state to be in and stay there
Observe the state a conversation is in, draw the two arrows of any single transaction, and see the repeating shape when the same ulterior transaction pays off between the same people over time
Diagnose strangers more efficiently

explanation.gentle: The first chapter gives you state observation. The second gives you the relational arrow diagram. This chapter gives you the second-layer structure and the repeating-pattern definition. Together they let you move from noticing a voice to diagramming an exchange to seeing the pattern a relationship keeps running. Picking the best state is the move the first chapter already said you cannot make. Diagnosing strangers more efficiently is the hammer problem.
explanation.direct: Three layers of tool, combined: state observation, arrow diagram, pattern shape. Picking a state misreads the first chapter. Stranger-diagnosis is the hammer problem this chapter warns against.
explanation.competitive: Layered diagnostic stack from state to vector to pattern is what the three chapters give you. Picking the best state is the move the first chapter said was unavailable. Diagnosing strangers is exactly the weaponization this chapter warns against, and answering that way means missing the whole point of the sequence.

keyTakeawayCard.gentle: Some transactions have two levels. When the second one repeats between the same people with the same shape, Berne called it a game. Every game has four nameable parts. Seeing the game is always valuable; breaking it is a separate and sometimes expensive decision.
keyTakeawayCard.direct: Ulterior transactions run on two levels. Games are repeated ulterior transactions with a nameable four-part anatomy. The anatomy is diagnostic, not prescriptive, and the antithesis costs the player the payoff they have been using.

chapters.title: Why Games Feel So Hard to Stop

chapterBreakdown.gentle: You probably already know the relationship that should not still be running and somehow is. The same painful argument every Sunday, the same late-night phone call, the same angry message from a stranger that ruins your morning. Berne built a small theory for why those patterns are so hard to leave. Human beings need a steady supply of social acknowledgment to stay functional. He called the unit a stroke. Strokes can be positive (a smile, a thanks, a real conversation) or negative (a fight, a criticism, an angry message). The hard, structural fact is that a negative stroke is metabolically better than no stroke at all. The painful pattern is sticky because it is paying both people in strokes they cannot get any other way, and because it is also confirming a position each of them has been holding since they were small.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Berne proposed two underlying reasons that games are sticky even after both players can see them. The first is strokes. A stroke is the basic unit of social acknowledgment that humans need to keep functioning. Positive strokes feel good; negative strokes feel bad; both register, and a negative stroke is metabolically better than no stroke at all. The second is life position. Every player carries a basic stance toward themselves and others, formed early. Berne named four: I'm OK and you're OK, I'm OK and you're not OK, I'm not OK and you're OK, I'm not OK and you're not OK. A game is sticky to the degree that it is the player's only reliable source of strokes AND it confirms their existing life position. Both have to be replaced before the game becomes possible to leave. The model is exact about that.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: In any pattern that has been running between two people for years and obviously hurting both of them, you are not looking at stupidity. moreDetails.direct: The player is solving a real problem with the only reliable tool they have found. The chapter's job is to name what the solution was solving, so the player has the option of building a less expensive one. It is not the chapter's job to take the solution away.

The chapter's job is to name what the solution was solving, so the player has the option of building a less expensive one. It is not the chapter's job to take the solution away. Internalize this now.

activationPrompt.gentle: Bring to mind a relationship that has been running on the same painful pattern for years. Try to name both legs: what strokes is the pattern paying each person, and what life position is each of them holding that the pattern keeps confirming?
activationPrompt.direct: Identify a multi-year painful pattern in your life. Name the strokes it pays both players and the life position it confirms for each. Be specific about both legs.
activationPrompt.competitive: Pick the longest-running painful pattern in your life. Name both legs in concrete terms. If you can name only one, you have not yet seen the reason it has lasted as long as it has.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: When did you most recently catch yourself accepting a negative stroke and recognizing, in real time, that you had taken it because the alternative was zero?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Name the most recent negative stroke you accepted. What was the zero-stroke alternative, and what made the negative one feel preferable?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Find the last time you took a negative stroke knowingly. Name the zero-stroke alternative. If you cannot remember the moment of choice, the stroke economy is running you instead of the other way around.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: What life position have you been holding since you were small that the games in your life have been confirming, and what would it cost to let it become slightly less true?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Identify your dominant life position. Name one game in your life that confirms it. Estimate, honestly, what it would cost to let the position update by even a small degree.
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Name your dominant life position. Identify the game that confirms it most reliably. Estimate the actual cost of letting the position update. The cost is the reason you have not.

predictionPrompt.gentle: If you spent two weeks deliberately collecting one positive stroke a day from a source you do not currently use, what do you predict would change in the painful patterns of your life by the end of those two weeks?
predictionPrompt.direct: Predict what would change in your most painful recurring pattern if, for two weeks, you added one reliable daily positive stroke from a source you do not currently use. Be specific about what would shift and what would not.
predictionPrompt.competitive: Run the experiment in your head: two weeks of one new positive stroke per day from a source you have not been using. What would the painful pattern in your life that you have already tried to leave look like after fourteen days? What would still be in place?

retrieve.gentle: Worth understanding: strokes (metabolic units of social acknowledgment) plus life positions (early-formed stances of the four kinds) explain why games are sticky. Negative strokes count. A game is sticky to the degree it pays strokes AND confirms a life position. Both legs reinforce each other.
retrieve.direct: Strokes (metabolic units of social acknowledgment) plus life positions (early-formed stances of the four kinds) explain why games are sticky. Negative strokes count. A game is sticky to the degree it pays strokes AND confirms a life position. Both legs reinforce each other.
retrieve.competitive: Strokes (metabolic units of social acknowledgment) plus life positions (early-formed stances of the four kinds) explain why games are sticky. Negative strokes count. A game is sticky to the degree it pays strokes AND confirms a life position. Both legs reinforce each other. This is the foundation.

This chapter names the expense in concrete terms (strokes plus position) and supplies the order of operations. Know this cold.

preview.direct: With the energetics in hand, the catalog of recurring patterns becomes readable. The next chapter starts with the long-running, biography-shaping games and applies the four-chapter stack to each one.

examples.title: Maya and the monthly angry GitHub issue

scenario.gentle: Maya is sitting at her kitchen table on Thursday morning with her laptop open to the GitHub issues page for the small parsing library she has maintained for seven years. The new issue at the top is angry. The stranger who opened it has not read the contributing guide and is accusing her of not caring. Maya hates the issue. She also notices, before her second cup of coffee, that the months when no angry issue arrives are the worse months, and she does not yet have a word for why. The issue is paying her something. The something is the wrong shape and she is taking it anyway.
scenario.direct: Thursday morning. Kitchen table, laptop, GitHub issues page for Maya's seven-year-old parsing library. New issue at the top: three paragraphs of unfounded accusation from a stranger. Maya reads it for the third time. Behind her conscious annoyance, the structural fact is filing itself: the issue is a stroke. Negative, hostile, unfair, and a stroke. Months without the issue feel worse than months with it.
scenario.competitive: The angry GitHub issue arrives roughly once a month, from strangers who have not read the contributing guide, accusing Maya of not caring about a library that almost nobody uses. Maya hates the issues. Maya also knows, in the part of herself she does not look at directly, that a month with no issue is a month in which her library has registered to no one and she has registered along with it. The negative stroke is doing the load-bearing work of a positive stroke she has not built a reliable source for.

whatToDo.gentle: The first move is not to delete the GitHub account or stop maintaining the library. Both of those are exit moves. The first move is to find one positive stroke source you can put on a weekly schedule before you do anything about the negative one. Join one small community where you can talk about the work. Send one piece of work to one person who will respond. Replace before you remove.
whatToDo.direct: Replace before remove. Schedule one weekly source of positive strokes (a writing group, a peer review session, a real conversation with another maintainer) before doing anything about the negative ones. The negative strokes can stay until the positive ones are arriving on a reliable schedule. Then they can be left.
whatToDo.competitive: Build the replacement supply first. One weekly source of positive strokes that arrives on a calendar. Then, and only then, mute the angry issues. Removing the negative supply before the positive supply is in place is starvation, not freedom, and you will return to the GitHub page within a fortnight.

whyItMatters.gentle: Solo creators are particularly vulnerable to negative-stroke economies because their work is solitary and the audience is mostly silent. Replacing the negative supply with a positive one on a schedule is the single most effective intervention available.
whyItMatters.direct: Solo creative work has a structural stroke-deficit problem because the audience is mostly silent. Negative strokes from strangers fill the gap reliably and are exhausting. Replacement is the only honest fix.
whyItMatters.competitive: Solo creators who do not build a positive stroke schedule for themselves end up dependent on negative strokes from strangers, and the dependency is invisible until somebody asks why they cannot stop reading the issues. The replacement schedule is the single intervention that scales.

scenario.gentle: It is 9:45 on a Tuesday night and Olu is standing in the linoleum hallway of the hospice unit between two patient rooms. She is thinking about the way she answered the question her supervisor asked her at change of shift, which was whether she could pick up another double on Friday, and about the way her mouth said yes before her brain reached the question. She is thinking that the patient in 207 told her three times tonight that she was an angel, and about how much the word 'angel' had mattered to her even though she does not believe in angels. She is noticing that the double on Friday is not about the unit. It is about hearing the word 'angel' three more times.
scenario.direct: 9:45 PM Tuesday. Olu, hospice nurse, linoleum hallway between rooms 207 and 209. Inner monologue: she just agreed to a Friday double without thinking. The patient in 207 called her an angel three times tonight. The word 'angel' is the stroke. The double is the way to get more of them. The structure is visible to her tonight in a way it has not been in the eighteen months she has worked the unit.
scenario.competitive: Tuesday night, 9:45 PM, hospice second floor. Olu just said yes to a Friday double she does not have the energy for. The patient in 207 called her an angel three times tonight, and Olu, watching herself from a small distance for the first time in eighteen months, sees that 'angel' is the stroke and the doubles are the way she has been arranging her life around getting more of them. She has nothing against the patient. She has nothing against the doubles. She has just noticed, on a linoleum hallway between two rooms, that her schedule has been organized by a stroke economy she did not choose.

whatToDo.gentle: When you catch yourself running a stroke-collection pattern at work, the first move is not to stop. It is to write down, in one sentence, what the stroke is and what it is paying for. Then, before you change anything, find one place in your week outside of work that could pay the same kind of stroke. The work can stay; the dependence on the work as the only source is what makes it expensive.
whatToDo.direct: Write down the stroke and the payoff. 'I am taking the doubles to be called an angel three times a shift.' Then identify one source of similar strokes outside of work. Until that source exists, do not cut the doubles.
whatToDo.competitive: Name the stroke. 'Angel, three times a shift, 36 hours a week.' Then build one source of the same kind of recognition outside of work. Until that source is paying you, the doubles are load-bearing and removing them is starvation.

whyItMatters.gentle: Helping professions are stroke-rich workplaces, which is why the people in them often discover, late, that their entire stroke supply is coming from work. The recognition is uncomfortable. The replacement is slow and worth it.
whyItMatters.direct: Helping professions are over-represented in stroke-economy patterns because the work itself is stroke-paying. Practitioners who do not build a parallel supply outside the work end up structurally dependent on the work for non-work reasons.
whyItMatters.competitive: Helping professions are stroke-rich and the practitioners in them are statistically the most likely to discover, decades in, that the work has been doing all of their social acknowledgment for them. The replacement supply is the single intervention that prevents the late-career collapse most outsiders cannot explain.

examples.title: Coach Park and Bailey in the robotics workshop

scenario.gentle: Coach Park is sitting on the edge of a workbench in the high-school robotics workshop with Bailey, a sixteen-year-old who has been the center of three escalating arguments with teammates this month. The competition robot is half-built on the bench between them. Coach Park is trying to figure out how to talk to Bailey about what she thinks she is seeing, which is that Bailey starts the arguments because the arguments are the only times any of his teammates pay full attention to him. The vocabulary 'stroke' is not going to land with a sixteen-year-old. She has to find a different way in.
scenario.direct: Robotics workshop after school. Coach Park sits on a workbench with Bailey (16, three escalating teammate conflicts this month). The half-built competition robot between them. Park's diagnosis: Bailey is starting the arguments because the arguments are the only moments of full attention from teammates he gets. She needs a way to say that without using the word 'stroke' and without sounding like a therapist.
scenario.competitive: Coach Park has eight minutes before the bus and Bailey has not been pulled into a teacher's office in two weeks, which means tonight is the only window. The robot is half-built on the bench. Bailey has been at the center of three arguments this month, and Park has watched all three closely enough to see the same shape under each: Bailey starts the argument when the room has been quiet for too long. The arguments are how he is being seen. Park has to hand him that diagnosis without using a single word from the book it came out of.

whatToDo.gentle: Park sits down at Bailey's level and asks, 'What is the best part of the arguments?' She does not ask why he starts them or whether he should stop. She asks what is good about them. Then she waits. The question has to come from genuine curiosity or the conversation will not survive Bailey's first eyeroll.
whatToDo.direct: Ask 'what is the best part of the arguments?' Wait for the answer. Bailey, if asked from real curiosity, will eventually say 'people pay attention.' Then ask: 'Where else in your week do people pay you that kind of attention?' Park does not have to name the stroke economy for it to do its work.
whatToDo.competitive: Three sentences only. 'Bailey, what is the best part of the arguments?' Wait. He'll say 'people listen' or 'they actually look at me.' Then: 'Where else in your week does that happen?' He'll say nothing. That nothing is the diagnosis, and it is now in his hands instead of yours.

whyItMatters.gentle: Sixteen-year-olds will refuse adult vocabulary about their feelings and accept structural questions about what they are getting out of a pattern. The structural question hands them a tool they can use without admitting weakness.
whyItMatters.direct: Adolescents reject self-help vocabulary on principle and accept structural questions about what they are getting out of a behavior. The structural question is the only intervention that survives adolescent skepticism.
whyItMatters.competitive: An adolescent who is handed a stroke-economy question instead of a feelings question will sometimes answer honestly. The honest answer is the only thing that will give the adult in the room a real next move. Therapy talk closes the door.

examples.title: Ahmed and Sun-Hee in the cohort study room

scenario.gentle: Ahmed and Sun-Hee are at the same table in the graduate cohort study room on a Wednesday evening. Ahmed has been describing, for the third time this week, how impossibly hard the methods chapter is and how little he is sleeping. Sun-Hee has been listening. Then she says, in a careful tone, 'Ahmed, I notice you tell me that the methods chapter is impossibly hard about every other day. What do you get out of the telling?' Ahmed's mouth opens and closes.
scenario.direct: AHMED (Wednesday evening, cohort study room, third hour): The methods chapter is impossibly hard. I'm not sleeping. SUN-HEE (carefully, after a pause): I notice you've told me that about every other day. What do you get out of the telling? AHMED: ... I do not know how to answer that question.
scenario.competitive: Ahmed had been describing the impossibility of the methods chapter for the third time this week. Sun-Hee listened until he finished, then said, 'What do you get out of telling me that?' Ahmed's first response was to feel attacked. His second response was to notice that he had no answer. His third response was to suspect that the answer was the answer to a question he had not been asking himself.

whatToDo.gentle: When somebody you trust asks you what you get out of a recurring complaint, the wrong move is to defend the complaint. The right move is to take the question seriously for thirty seconds and try to answer it. The answer is usually some form of 'attention' or 'permission to be unwell,' and naming it is the entire intervention.
whatToDo.direct: Take the question seriously for thirty seconds. The answer to 'what do you get out of the telling' is usually 'someone listens' or 'I am allowed to be struggling' or 'it justifies how tired I am.' Naming the answer is the intervention.
whatToDo.competitive: Answer the question honestly to yourself within thirty seconds, before your defenses arrive. The answer is what the recurring complaint has been paying you. Naming it does not stop you from making the complaint. It does change what the next telling can be about.

whyItMatters.gentle: Recurring complaint patterns inside graduate cohorts are quietly expensive because the cohort listens forever and the listener supply runs low. Catching the pattern in a friendly cohort is one of the cheapest places to learn about your own stroke economy.
whyItMatters.direct: Recurring complaint patterns in cohort settings get noticed first by the friend who stops finding them interesting and gets named, if at all, by the friend who is brave enough to ask the structural question. Both are gifts.
whyItMatters.competitive: A graduate student who can hear the question 'what do you get out of the telling' without flinching is six months ahead of their cohort on the work most of the cohort will not do until therapy in their thirties. The question is short and the cost of refusing it is years.

scenario.gentle: It is 11:08pm on a Thursday and the cup of tea on my counter is cold. My phone is in my hand. The screen has Coach Banerjee's name on it because I have started typing her name into the search bar three times this evening. The crisis is real. It is also the third real crisis this week, and I am beginning to notice that the third real crisis this week is not unusual for me. I am noticing it because, for the first time, I can see that the call is also a stroke, and that I have been arranging my Thursdays around getting one.
scenario.direct: 11:08 PM Thursday. Cold tea, phone in hand, Coach Banerjee's name typed into the search bar for the third time tonight. First-person inner monologue: the crisis is real and the call is a stroke. Both are true. Decision: place the call, name the pattern out loud to Banerjee, or close the phone and write down what I would have said.
scenario.competitive: 11:08 PM. Cold tea. My phone with Banerjee's name on it for the third time tonight. The crisis is real. The call is also the third call this week, and I am noticing tonight, for the first time, that I have been arranging my evenings around it. The window in front of me is about three minutes wide. After that I will either have called or not called, and either way the recognition will start to fade.

whatToDo.gentle: Before you make the call, write down the one thing you would have said. One sentence, on paper or on your phone notes. Then sit with it for two minutes. Sometimes you will still need to call. Sometimes the writing will turn out to be most of what the call was for, and you will not need it tonight. Either way you will know more than you knew before.
whatToDo.direct: Write the sentence first. One sentence of what you would have said. Sit with it for two minutes. Decide after the two minutes whether to call. The writing is the experiment that tells you which strokes the call was actually paying.
whatToDo.competitive: Write the sentence before you call. One sentence, on the same phone you were going to call her with. Two minutes of silence. If you still want to call after the two minutes, call, but call from a different place than the one you were calling from before. If you do not want to call, you have learned what the call was paying you.

whyItMatters.gentle: Late-night crisis calls inside long friendships are stroke economies in costume. The two-minute writing intervention is the one thing that works because it gives the strokes a different shape to live in.
whyItMatters.direct: The two-minute writing intervention works because it satisfies the part of the brain that wanted contact without spending the friendship. The call can still happen; the dependency is what shifts.
whyItMatters.competitive: Long friendships that turn into crisis-call schedules end one of two ways: they collapse under the weight of the calls, or one of the two friends learns to write the sentence first. There is no third option that does not eventually become one of the first two.

examples.title: Theo driving home from Ren's house

scenario.gentle: Theo is driving home from his daughter Ren's house on a Sunday evening, going slowly, with the radio off. He is reconstructing the visit. He always reconstructs the visit. The visit started at one with him bringing the kids those cookies they like. The visit ended at four with Ren saying, in the careful voice she has been using since she had her own kids, 'Dad, please. Please don't tell me how to do this.' He had told her how to do something. He always tells her how to do something. He is sixty-eight years old and he has told women in his family how to do things since 1962, and every time he does it, the room briefly contains him in a way that the rest of his life does not. He does not have a different way to be in a room yet.
scenario.direct: Sunday evening, Theo driving home from Ren's house. Radio off. He is reconstructing the visit. Pattern: he arrives, he eventually criticizes something Ren is doing with the kids, Ren tells him to stop, he says he is sorry, he leaves. The criticism is the moment he is most fully present in the room. He has been doing some version of this since 1962, and the criticism is the only role that has ever made him feel necessary in a room of women.
scenario.competitive: Theo's Sunday-evening drive home is the only honest hour he gives himself all week. He uses it to reconstruct the visit. The visit always ends with Ren asking him to stop telling her how to raise her kids. He always says he is sorry. He always does it again. He has been running the same shape since 1962, and the criticism is the only move he has ever found that makes a room of women look at him long enough for him to feel he is in it. He is sixty-eight. He does not have a replacement, and the absence of a replacement is the entire reason next Sunday will look exactly like this Sunday.

whatToDo.gentle: When you find yourself at the end of a long-running pattern with someone you love, the move is not to confess. The move is to find, for the next week, one other place where the same kind of presence is possible without the criticism. A volunteer commitment, a class, a long walk with an old friend. Build the replacement first. The criticism becomes possible to leave only after the replacement is paying.
whatToDo.direct: Find one weekly source of the same kind of being-needed without the criticism. Volunteer at a community garden, take a class, schedule a long weekly call with an old friend. Until that source pays, do not promise Ren you will stop. The promise without the replacement will not survive the next Sunday.
whatToDo.competitive: Replace before you promise. One weekly source of being-needed that does not require criticism. Until it exists, the promise to Ren is a check that will bounce next Sunday. The replacement is the only honest gift you can give your daughter.

whyItMatters.gentle: Long-running family patterns are the hardest stroke economies to leave because the strokes have been arriving in the same room for decades. The replacement supply is the only intervention that lasts.
whyItMatters.direct: Family stroke economies are the longest-running and the hardest to interrupt because the source is irreplaceable in the player's mind. The replacement supply has to be built outside the family for the inside to become possible to change.
whyItMatters.competitive: A retired man who finds one weekly volunteer commitment that pays him strokes outside his daughter's house has changed the next twenty Sundays for both of them. A retired man who keeps trying to stop without a replacement has changed nothing, and his daughter knows it.

questions.prompt: In Berne's model, what does the word 'stroke' refer to?
choices: Any positive emotion
A specific therapeutic technique
The basic unit of social acknowledgment that humans need to keep functioning

explanation.gentle: Berne uses 'stroke' in a specific technical sense: the basic unit of social acknowledgment a human needs to stay psychologically functional. It is not just a positive emotion (the chapter is explicit that negative strokes count too), and it is not a therapeutic technique. It is the metabolic unit the rest of the chapter rests on.
explanation.direct: Acknowledgment is the right answer because Berne defines strokes as units of social acknowledgment, neutral on whether they are positive or negative. Calling it a positive emotion misses the negative-strokes-count claim. Calling it a therapeutic technique misreads the noun as a verb.
explanation.competitive: Acknowledgment is the unit. The 'positive emotion' answer collapses the chapter's central distinction; the 'therapeutic technique' answer confuses Berne's noun for a stroke (the unit) with the verb to stroke (the action). Neither has the structural claim the chapter rests on.

questions.prompt: Why does Berne argue a negative stroke (a fight, an angry message, a criticism) is metabolically better than no stroke at all?
choices: Because the human nervous system needs a steady supply of acknowledgment, and any acknowledgment registers as evidence of being seen, even when the content is bad
Because negative strokes build character
Because conflict is stimulating

explanation.gentle: The chapter is structural here, not moralistic. The need for acknowledgment is metabolic, and a negative stroke arrives in a metabolism that would otherwise have received zero arrivals that day. The character-building answer is a moralization the chapter explicitly refuses, and the stimulation answer makes the negative stroke sound recreational.
explanation.direct: Metabolic acknowledgment is the chapter's claim. The character-building answer turns a structural fact into a moral story. The stimulation answer makes the negative stroke sound like entertainment, which trivializes the energetics.
explanation.competitive: Metabolism, not character, not entertainment. The chapter's structural claim is what makes the rest of the model work; the alternative answers both turn the structural claim into something more comfortable, which is exactly the misread the chapter is built to refuse.

questions.prompt: Maya, the open-source maintainer, reads her monthly angry GitHub issue from a stranger and notices that the months without an angry issue are the worse months. According to the chapter, what is the angry issue paying her?
choices: Practice in handling criticism
A negative stroke that is doing the work of a positive stroke she does not have a reliable source for, plus a confirmation of her existing life position
Information about her library's user base

explanation.gentle: The chapter is specific: the angry issue is paying Maya in two reinforcing ways. First, a negative stroke that arrives in a stroke-deficit environment and is metabolically registered as acknowledgment. Second, a confirmation of the position she has been holding since middle school. The 'practice' answer moralizes; the 'information' answer mistakes the social-level content of the issue for what is actually being delivered.
explanation.direct: Stroke plus position confirmation is the structural answer. Practice in criticism turns the answer into a self-improvement story; reading the issue as user research mistakes the content for the payoff.
explanation.competitive: Stroke and position. The practice answer turns the chapter into a personal-growth story, which it is not. The user-research answer reads the surface and misses the entire ulterior level the previous chapter introduced.

questions.prompt: Theo, the retired schoolteacher, criticizes his adult daughter Ren's parenting every Sunday despite apologizing every week and being asked to stop. Which life position is the criticism most likely confirming?
choices: I'm OK / You're OK
I'm not OK / You're OK
I'm OK / You're not OK

explanation.gentle: The chapter places Theo in I'm OK / You're not OK. He has been holding the position 'you have to point out what is wrong or nothing will get fixed' since 1962. The criticism is the move that keeps the position alive. I'm OK / You're OK is the healthy stance and is incompatible with running a Sunday criticism game; I'm not OK / You're OK is depressive and martyr-like, which Theo's posture is not.
explanation.direct: I'm OK / You're not OK is the structural fit. Theo's stance is corrective and projective, not depressive or healthy. The chapter is explicit that the criticism move is the position-confirming machinery.
explanation.competitive: Projective, not depressive, not healthy. Theo is running the position from a place of correctness. The other answers misread the energy of the criticism as either martyrdom or game-free contact, both of which the chapter explicitly distinguishes.

questions.prompt: Inez calls her friend Banerjee at 11pm with what is now the third real crisis this week. According to the chapter, what is the relationship-level stroke economy paying both women?
choices: Inez gets reliable late-night attention from a person who has known her since college, and Banerjee gets confirmation that she is the kind of person who can be called at 11pm with a crisis, which is one of the only places in her week anybody needs anything from her in particular
Banerjee is doing all the giving
Inez is exploiting the friendship and Banerjee should set a boundary

explanation.gentle: The chapter's point is that both women are getting paid by the loop. The 'Banerjee is doing all the giving' answer treats the rescuer role as costless to the rescuer, which it is not. The 'set a boundary' answer is from a different framework and misses the chapter's structural point that the calls are paying Banerjee strokes she has not built another source for.
explanation.direct: Two-sided payout is the chapter's structural claim. One-sided exploitation misreads the energetics; boundary language imports a different framework and mistakes the symptom for the structure.
explanation.competitive: Both sides are getting paid. Treating Banerjee as a victim ignores what the rescuer role is paying her. Treating it as a boundary problem skips the energetic question the chapter is built to ask.

questions.prompt: A reader sees the position 'I'm not OK / You're OK' and concludes it is just a fancy term for self-criticism. Why does the chapter resist that reading?
choices: Because self-criticism is actually rare

Because 'I'm not OK / You're OK' is the deeper structural stance behind self-criticism, formed early and confirmed daily by the kinds of transactions the player participates in, and dislodging it requires updating the position itself, not just changing the visible behavior
Because the position is genetic

explanation.gentle: The chapter is careful here. Self-criticism is the visible behavior; the position is the deeper stance the behavior is expressing. Treating them as the same thing leads to interventions that target the visible behavior and fail because the position is still doing the underlying work. The chapter is not making a claim about how rare self-criticism is, and it is explicit that life positions are formed by experience, not genetics.
explanation.direct: Position-vs-behavior distinction is the chapter's point. Self-criticism rarity is irrelevant to the question; genetic claims are explicitly outside the chapter's framework.
explanation.competitive: Behavior is the surface, position is the structure. Confusing them is how the entire self-help industry has been failing readers for sixty years. The other answers misread the chapter's frame entirely.

questions.prompt: A senior manager named Mei is the only one in her company who works late on Friday nights and has been doing so for six years. She tells her partner she would love to leave on time. Identify the most likely stroke and life position the pattern is confirming.
choices: Stroke: overtime pay. Position: I'm not OK / You're not OK
Stroke: career advancement. Position: I'm OK / You're OK

Stroke: a reliable supply of being-noticed by the late-night office cleaning crew and the one other workaholic on her floor, plus the messages from her boss the next morning. Position: I am not OK unless I am the one who stays the latest

explanation.gentle: The chapter's transfer move asks the reader to read for the actual stroke (the small reliable acknowledgments that arrive on the late-night schedule) and the actual position (the I'm not OK that requires the hours to stay confirmed). The first wrong answer reads the surface (pay) and misses the energetics. The second is incompatible with a six-year reluctant pattern.
explanation.direct: Reliable late-night acknowledgment plus an I'm-not-OK-without-the-hours position is the structural read. Overtime pay misses the energetics; career advancement misreads the felt experience of the pattern.
explanation.competitive: Late-night acknowledgment plus position-confirmation is the answer. The pay answer reads the surface; the career-advancement answer is incompatible with the reluctance the manager is reporting.

questions.prompt: If Maya wanted to stop running her angry-GitHub-issue game, which of the following is the chapter actually recommending she do?
choices: Delete the GitHub repository and find a new hobby

Schedule one reliable weekly source of positive strokes (a writing group, a peer review, a real conversation with another maintainer) before doing anything about the negative ones, then slowly work on the position the negative strokes have been confirming
Force herself to stop reading the issues and accept the discomfort

explanation.gentle: The chapter's order of operations is replacement first, then exit. Deleting the repo is exit without replacement, and the chapter is explicit that exit without replacement leads to deprivation and return. Forcing herself to stop reading is the same instruction in a different costume. The reliable replacement supply is the only honest first move.

Greta has been signing the same business partnership since her twenties. Felix has been collecting his colleagues' procedural lapses for twenty years and releasing them on a schedule. chapterBreakdown.gentle:
Most of the patterns the previous chapters described run in a single conversation, or a single relationship, or at most a single recurring weekly meeting or setting. Life games are different. They run on a biographical scale: years, sometimes whole decades. The same opening move, the same predictable response, the same switch, the same payoff, distributed across the player's entire working life.

Greta is sitting at a coffee table signing the fourth partnership agreement of her career. Each of the previous three partnerships ended the same way: a partner who was generous and excited at signing turned out, six months in, to take more than their share. Greta describes each ending as bad luck. The fourth one is going to end the same way because the pattern is not luck. The thesis of her game is exploitability: she makes herself easy to take from, somebody takes, and the position she has been holding since her twenties (the world will take what it can take) is confirmed one more time. The strokes are the small reliable acknowledgment of being seen as generous and put-upon afterward. The dynamics are her need for the position to stay confirmed.

Felix is the head of a department at a regional hospital and runs a different pattern. He has been collecting his colleagues' procedural lapses in a private file for years, then waiting for one of them to make an unambiguous mistake before releasing the stored anger of all the previous lapses as a justified, technically-correct response. The thesis is the collection plus the release. The antithesis is a colleague who is so impeccable in their work that Felix's file stays empty. The dynamics are Felix's need to keep the position confirmed that he is the only one in the room with standards. The payoff is the moral charge of guilt-free anger plus the strokes of being feared as the standards-keeper. The chapter does not use Berne's name for this pattern. The structure is the lesson.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne placed life games at the deepest level of his catalog because they are the longest-running cases the model handles. They are biographical, not local: they run on a multi-year schedule, organizing the player's whole working life. The same opening move, the same predictable response, the same switch, the same payoff, distributed across years rather than across an afternoon.

The chapter walks through four patterns. The exploitability pattern is Greta's: she signs a generous business partnership, makes herself easy to take from, gets taken from, and describes the ending as bad luck. The position confirmed is that the world takes what it can. The righteous-outrage pattern is Felix's: a department head who collects his colleagues' procedural lapses for months and then releases the stored anger as a justified, technically-correct response. The position confirmed is that he is the only one in the room with standards. The displaced-blame pattern is Ivar's: a project coordinator who explains every mistake on every project as the consequence of the colleague who interrupted him at the critical moment. The position confirmed is that he never causes the things that go wrong. He has worked in the same coordinator role at three different organizations and the pattern has run identically at all three, down to the same timing and the same switching move. A fourth pattern is Mona's, which shares structural features with both Greta's and Ivar's: she takes on more work than she can complete at rates she cannot sustain, then proves nothing can be done about it. Each new client confirms the position: the demands are real, the time is genuinely short, and the arrangement could not have worked.

All four have the four-part anatomy from the third chapter and the stickiness equation from the fourth, applied at biographical scale. The new claim, and the only one this chapter actually cares about, is the time horizon. The antithesis to a life game is not a single conversation. It is a multi-year project requiring a new stroke supply and a slow update of the position the pattern has been confirming for decades.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The reason the catalog starts here is structural. Life games are the deepest cases the model handles, and the reader who has just learned the four-chapter stack will be tempted to try it on the smaller games of the next chapters first, where the time horizons are kinder. Berne resists that temptation by placing the longest-arc cases first, and by walking through them in detail.

Greta runs a small graphic design studio and is signing her fourth partnership agreement in a career that has been running the same opening move since her twenties. The previous three partnerships all ended the same way: she made herself easy to take from, somebody took, and the position she has been holding since her twenties got proven one more time. Felix is the head of a department at a regional hospital and has been collecting procedural lapses from his colleagues for twenty years, releasing them on a schedule of his own as justified, technically-correct outrage. Ivar is a project coordinator who has been explaining every mistake as the fault of the colleague who interrupted him at the critical moment. Mona is a freelancer who has been taking on more work than she can complete at rates she cannot sustain for ten years and proving nothing can be done about it. Each new client confirms it in the same way.

All four have the four-part anatomy from the third chapter and the stickiness equation from the fourth, distributed across years instead of conversations. The leverage in the chapter, and the only honest piece of advice it offers, is the time horizon. The antithesis to a thirty-year game is not a sentence. It is a project. A reader who watches Greta's antithesis-partner refuse to exploit her, and watches Greta find another partner who will, has watched the model do exactly what the model is supposed to do at the right time scale. The model is fine. The time scale is the part most readers use wrong.

The antithesis would be a partner who declines to take, treats her generously, and watches Greta find another partner who will.
