chapterBreakdown.gentle:
There is a way to spend an evening with a room full of people and leave without having been genuinely present with any of them, and for most people it is the default. Party games are the catalog entry for that default. They are short, social, produce real warmth, and cost each player almost nothing personally because they are organized around a shared stance toward something outside the group.

Berne's Ain't It Awful is the most structurally efficient of the three. A group deplores something: publishing, politicians, the economy. The content is real. The structure is the most complementary transaction possible: mutual agreement. No one has to say anything particular about themselves. The pattern can run for years in a book club without any member deciding to run it. The antithesis breaks the loop with a question that requires an individual response: 'What would you actually do?' It is uncomfortable because it requires someone to step out of the shared stance.

Why Don't You Yes But is the hardest to interrupt because the advice-giving social contract makes refusing to advise seem rude. Five suggestions, five technically accurate rejections. The colleagues leave feeling subtly incompetent. The player leaves having proved insolubility and collected the strokes. The payoff is dual. The antithesis refuses the generator role and hands the problem back: 'What have you already tried?' Slightly rude. Almost always more productive than the fourth suggestion.

Blemish is the most socially subtle. Cass finds a flaw in every piece, first, before any strength is noted. The flaws are genuine. The game is in the sequencing and consistency, producing social superiority through technical accuracy that cannot be disputed. The antithesis acknowledges the flaw and names strengths, declining the sequencing contest without disputing the finding.

The chapter's hardest claim is the limit. Not all of these activities are games. The dynamics distinguish: is the activity moving or circling? A book club that deplores for thirty-eight minutes and has been having the same conversation for three years is circling. A team meeting that deplores for fifteen minutes and produces an action item is not a game; it is processing. The WDYYB is a game when the player's goal is not a solution but the proof of insolubility. When someone is genuinely stuck and hoping a suggestion lands, the pattern is not WDYYB even if the suggestions fail. The model is a reading tool, not a filter, and using it as a filter produces the hammer problem from Chapter 3 at social scale.

A careful reader will notice that all three patterns described here are running inside settings that are otherwise healthy. The book club is not dysfunctional. The team meeting is not a broken organization. The critique session is not a hostile environment. The games run inside all of them because healthy social containers provide the obligation that makes refusing to participate feel impolite.

That is the chapter's unsentimental observation: the games are solving a real problem. They provide warmth, structure, and social contact without requiring anyone to be genuinely vulnerable. The antithesis does not eliminate that problem. It makes the problem visible and offers the room the option of choosing differently. Most rooms will not take it. The chapter does not expect them to, and does not treat that as a failure. The observation alone is worth something.

scenario.gentle: Pita is at the kitchen table at 10:30am describing a client scope problem to Nneka and Haruto. Three colleagues, three suggestions, three rejections. Each rejection is technically accurate. Haruto has a fourth suggestion ready and is deciding whether to offer it.
scenario.direct: NNEKA: Can you set a hard limit in the next call? PITA: Yes, but they will feel I am being unresponsive. HARUTO: Renegotiate the contract? PITA: Yes, but that could damage the relationship. NNEKA: Document what is out of scope? PITA: Yes, but I tried that and it did not land. Haruto has a fourth suggestion. He has not offered it yet.
scenario.competitive: Three suggestions, three technically accurate rejections. Haruto is looking at the exchange and calculating whether his fourth suggestion will follow the pattern of the first three. He already knows the answer.

whatToDo.gentle: Stop after the second rejection and ask: 'Pita, what have you already tried, in your own words?' That question exits the generator role and hands the problem back.
whatToDo.direct: Refuse the generator role after the second rejection. Ask: 'What would you actually try if you had to?' One question. It is the antithesis and it ends the loop faster than any number of suggestions.
whatToDo.competitive: After the second rejection, ask: 'What would you do if I were not here?' One question. The loop ends or it reveals itself. Either outcome is more useful than a fourth suggestion.

whyItMatters.gentle: Colleagues who stay in the rejection loop after two declines are providing raw material for rejections, not solutions. The antithesis question costs one sentence.
whyItMatters.direct: The WDYYB pattern uses colleagues as proof-generators. Each suggestion provides material for a new confirmation of insolubility. The antithesis breaks the loop with one question.
whyItMatters.competitive: Every suggestion after the second is a stroke paid to the game. The antithesis question is the move that ends the loop, exits the generator role, and puts the problem back where it belongs.

scenario.gentle: It is the monthly retrospective and I have agreed with Faye three times in twenty minutes that the timelines are unrealistic. I agree. The timelines are unrealistic. I have been agreeing with variations of this for three retrospectives and nothing about our timelines has changed.
scenario.direct: Monthly retrospective. Three agreements with Faye about timelines in twenty minutes. Three months of the same pattern. Zero changes to timelines. I am asking myself, right now, what it would actually take to change a timeline, and I realize I have not asked that question once in three months of retrospectives.
scenario.competitive: I have been Faye's agreement-provider on the timeline problem for three retrospectives. The problem is real. The agreeing is real. The agreeing has not moved the problem anywhere. I am deciding whether to agree a fourth time or ask the question.

whatToDo.gentle: The next sentence is a question, not an agreement. 'What would we actually need to change to set a realistic timeline in the next project?' The question converts deploring-in-place into the beginning of a plan.
whatToDo.direct: Stop agreeing. Ask: 'What specific change would we make to set a realistic timeline?' The question is the antithesis. It breaks the loop.
whatToDo.competitive: Ask the question before the fourth agreement. 'What specifically would we change, and who owns that change?' One question. If Faye answers, the loop becomes a plan.

whyItMatters.gentle: A retrospective that spends twenty minutes deploring timelines without producing one change to how timelines are set has been an AIA session in a meeting room. The antithesis question converts it.
whyItMatters.direct: Deploring-in-place without producing change is the AIA pattern in a professional setting. The antithesis question costs nothing and converts the session from circling to moving.
whyItMatters.competitive: Twenty minutes of agreement on a problem that does not change is twenty minutes of stroke delivery to a loop. The antithesis question is free and ends the loop.

scenario.gentle: The student design critique has been running for forty minutes. Cass has reviewed six pieces. In all six, the first comment has been a flaw. The flaws have all been accurate. The other students have started presenting defensively. The energy in the room has been tightening for forty minutes.
scenario.direct: Design critique, second year. Six pieces, six first-comments from Cass, all of them accurate flaws. Students are preparing defensively. Three presenters remain. The session is fifteen minutes from the end and has been a competition to survive for forty minutes.
scenario.competitive: Cass has led with the flaw on all six pieces. All six findings were accurate. The class is now a room where learning has been replaced by defensive positioning. Three students are still waiting to present.

whatToDo.gentle: The instructor's move is to introduce a structure: two strengths before any critique. The rule changes the sequence without changing the content. Cass can still find the flaw; it just comes third.
whatToDo.direct: Introduce a sequencing rule before the next presenter: two strengths before any critique. The rule defeats the first-flaw positioning without requiring Cass to be called out. The game runs on sequencing; the rule changes the sequence.
whatToDo.competitive: Change the sequence now. 'New rule: two strengths before any critique.' The rule is the antithesis. It is impersonal. The sequencing contest is over.

whyItMatters.gentle: A critique room organized around surviving the first-flaw move is not a learning room. Changing the sequence changes what the room is for.
whyItMatters.direct: First-flaw positioning changes what students do: they defend rather than explore. The sequence rule restores the function.
whyItMatters.competitive: The critique room organized around Cass's first-flaw move is a competition room. The sequence rule ends the competition in one sentence.

scenario.gentle: Kira is a first-year teacher running morning check-ins that have become open complaint sessions. Students share difficulties; Kira validates each one. The check-ins are warm. At the end of six weeks, the same students are sharing the same problems every Monday and the problems are not getting smaller.
scenario.direct: Kira to Coach Mbeki: 'My morning check-ins are warm, students engage, but I think I might be running a deploring session. The same problems keep coming up and they do not go anywhere.' Mbeki recognizes the structure.
scenario.competitive: Coach Mbeki is looking at Kira's check-in design and seeing a well-intentioned AIA loop. Students are being validated into their problems rather than through them.

whatToDo.gentle: Mbeki asks: 'At the end of the check-in, is anything different for the student who shared, or does the problem look the same as when they started? If it looks the same, the check-in is providing comfort without movement.' Then help Kira add one forward question at the end of each share.
whatToDo.direct: Ask Kira: 'At the end of each share, has anything moved?' Then design one forward question to add to each check-in: 'What would one small better look like this week?' The check-in stays warm. The direction changes.
whatToDo.competitive: Give Kira the move. 'After each share, ask: what would one thing look different look like this week? One question. The check-in stays warm. The students leave with a place to go.' One sentence to Kira.

whyItMatters.gentle: Check-ins that provide validation without forward movement become stroke sources rather than growth tools. One forward question changes the direction without reducing the warmth.
whyItMatters.direct: Validation loops in classroom check-ins are genuine care with a design problem. The forward question is the fix.
whyItMatters.competitive: A check-in that students look forward to but that moves nothing is a stroke source, not a learning tool. One question turns it into both.

scenario.gentle: It is forty-three minutes into the October book club. The book is on the table. Leila has not read it, and did not read last month's either. She came for the conversation. The conversation is about publishing and schools and a politician. The conversation is warm. Leila is thinking about when the book became optional for her.
scenario.direct: Inner monologue, 43 minutes in. I have not read the last two books. I am here. The conversation is good. I have been agreeing with people for forty-three minutes and have not said anything specifically mine. I am thinking about why I keep coming.
scenario.competitive: Leila has not read the last two books and she is sitting at the table agreeing with people about things she also finds concerning and the room is warm and she is also aware that she could have this conversation with anyone and she is not quite having it with the specific people at this table.

whatToDo.gentle: The question Leila can ask herself is not for the room: what do I want this evening to be? If the answer includes the book, she can say so. If the answer is the conversation, she can stay in it deliberately. Either is valid. The passive participation is what is not.
whatToDo.direct: Decide what you want from the book club. Not in the abstract, but tonight. If you want the conversation, be in it deliberately. If you want the book, say so. The passive participation is the game you are running on yourself.
whatToDo.competitive: Make a decision before the next meeting: what you are there for. If it is the conversation, own it. If it is the book, say so. Three years of passive participation in a loop you have not been deciding to be in is three years of a choice unmade.

whyItMatters.gentle: Showing up to something without deciding what you want from it is how you end up in a loop for three years. The decision is small. The loop is long.
whyItMatters.direct: Passive participation in social loops that no longer serve the original purpose is how people organize their social time around routines rather than choices. The antithesis is a decision.
whyItMatters.competitive: Three years of the same conversation is three years of a choice you have not been making deliberately. Make it now, one way or the other.

scenario.gentle: Rowan is thinking, three weeks after the Saturday dinner, about the two hours spent talking about the housing market, a mutual friend, and the general direction of things. The dinner was warm. Rowan also came home feeling a hunger they could not immediately name. Looking at it now, the hunger was for something the dinner did not provide.
scenario.direct: Three weeks later. Rowan catalogs the topics: housing market, mutual acquaintance, general direction of things. Things specific to the people at the table: five minutes, mostly logistics. The warmth was real. The hunger afterward was also real.
scenario.competitive: Three weeks out, the dinner looks like: two hours of shared grievance, real warmth, and Rowan left hungry because nobody said anything specifically true about themselves for more than five minutes. Rowan is deciding whether to say something at the next dinner.

whatToDo.gentle: The move Rowan can make at the next dinner is small: say one specifically true thing about themselves that is not a complaint about the world. Not a big disclosure. Something specific and real. That move is the antithesis at the smallest possible scale.
whatToDo.direct: At the next dinner, say one specific true thing about yourself that is not a shared grievance. One sentence, about you, now, real. See what happens. The room will either respond or it will not. Either is information.
whatToDo.competitive: Say the specific true thing. One sentence about you at the next dinner. Not a complaint. Something real. The room responds or it does not. Either answer is information you do not currently have about what your friend group is for.

whyItMatters.gentle: The hunger after warmth-without-contact is real and it is information. It is telling you what the evening was not providing. The one specific true thing is the smallest move toward what the hunger was asking for.
whyItMatters.direct: Post-dinner hunger after warmth-without-genuine-contact is the reliable signal that the evening ran on agreement strokes. The antithesis is one specific true thing.
whyItMatters.competitive: The ratio of shared grievance to personal disclosure at your dinners is information about what your friend group is for. One sentence changes the ratio and tells you whether the group can hold it.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes party games from life games and marital games?
choices: Party games are more harmful because they run in groups
Party games are short-duration social patterns that provide warmth and bonding without genuine contact, at low individual cost per player
Party games are only run by extroverts

explanation.gentle: Scale and social function is the distinction. Party games are short-duration, low-individual-cost, and group-based. They are not more harmful than other games; they are less individually costly but socially expensive in aggregate.
explanation.direct: Short-duration, low-individual-cost, group-bonding without genuine contact is the category definition. Harm comparison and personality-type framing miss the structural argument.
explanation.competitive: Scale and social function define the category. Harm is not a comparative judgment the chapter makes. Personality is not a structural claim.

questions.prompt: What is the book club's thirty-eight-minute deploring providing to its members?
choices: An outlet for legitimate civic frustration
Social warmth through mutual agreement, without any of the members having to be genuinely present with each other
A productive introduction to the book discussion

explanation.gentle: Warmth without genuine presence is the payoff. Civic frustration outlet describes the content, not the function. Book introduction is falsified by the fact that three members have stopped reading.
explanation.direct: Warmth through agreement without personal exposure is the structural payoff. Civic outlet describes the content. Book discussion framing is empirically wrong.
explanation.competitive: Warmth through agreement is the payment. The content is civic; the function is stroke delivery without personal risk.

questions.prompt: In the kitchen WDYYB pattern, Pita presents a problem and rejects every suggestion. What is the pattern actually doing?
choices: Proving the problem is insoluble, which protects Pita from having to try any of the suggestions and delivers strokes from the colleagues' attempts
Genuinely seeking a solution but unable to find one
Trying to share emotional difficulty without asking directly for support

explanation.gentle: Proving insolubility is the psychological-level goal. The double payoff is strokes from attempts plus protection from trying. Genuine solution-seeking is falsified by the pattern. Emotional-sharing framing describes a different need.
explanation.direct: Insolubility proof plus strokes is the double payoff. Genuine seeking is falsified by the consistent rejection pattern. Emotional support framing is a different structure.
explanation.competitive: The rejection IS the goal, not the obstacle. Genuine seeking would take one suggestion. Emotional support framing does not account for the rejection sequence.

questions.prompt: What does Cass's consistent first-flaw move provide that is harder to get from other sources?
choices: Accurate feedback that other reviewers are too polite to give
Social superiority achieved through technical accuracy, which cannot be disputed because the flaws are real
Recognition from other students for having high standards

explanation.gentle: Undisputable positioning is the payoff. The accuracy is the vehicle; the sequencing is the game. Recognition is indirect and downstream.
explanation.direct: Undisputable social superiority through accurate findings is the specific payoff. Accuracy is the vehicle; the sequencing is the game. Recognition from others is downstream.
explanation.competitive: Undisputable social positioning through technical accuracy. Direct comparison can be challenged; accurate first-findings cannot.

questions.prompt: Nneka has just offered Pita a second rejected suggestion. What is the antithesis to the WDYYB loop?
choices: Offer a third, better suggestion
Ask: 'What would you actually try if you had to?' and refuse to offer another suggestion
Tell Pita that the pattern is called WDYYB

explanation.gentle: The hand-back question is the antithesis. A third suggestion extends the loop. Naming the game is a later, separate conversation.
explanation.direct: The hand-back question exits the generator role. Another suggestion is more material for the loop. Naming the game is a meta-conversation, not the kitchen move.
explanation.competitive: One question, refusing the generator role, is the antithesis. Third suggestion continues the loop. Naming the game might be useful later but is not the immediate move.

questions.prompt: How does the chapter say you can tell the difference between Ain't It Awful (a game) and genuine collective processing of a shared problem?
choices: By whether the dynamics are moving the conversation toward something (a plan, a decision, a new understanding) or circling in place over the same ground
By whether the content of the complaints is accurate
By how long the conversation has been going

explanation.gentle: Moving vs circling is the diagnostic. Accuracy of content is not the distinguishing feature: AIA runs on accurate complaints. Duration is not the distinguishing feature.
explanation.direct: Dynamics (moving or circling) is the only reliable diagnostic. Accuracy and duration are both present in the game and in the legitimate activity; only the direction of movement distinguishes them.
explanation.competitive: Moving vs circling is the distinction the chapter names explicitly. Accuracy and duration are not diagnostic. The game is the circling, not the content or the length.

questions.prompt: At a dinner party, a group spends ninety minutes discussing a mutual friend's poor decisions, all agreeing. Nobody offers a plan to help; nobody says anything personal. Which party game pattern does this match?
choices: Why Don't You Yes But, because they are rejecting each other's solutions
Blemish, because they are finding flaws in the friend
Ain't It Awful, because the group is bonding through shared deploring without moving toward action or personal disclosure

explanation.gentle: Shared deploring without movement is the AIA match. WDYYB requires a player seeking suggestions; no one is seeking advice here. Blemish requires sequential critique; this is group agreement.
explanation.direct: Mutual agreement deploring without movement is AIA. WDYYB needs suggestion-rejection structure. Blemish needs first-flaw sequencing in a critique context.
explanation.competitive: AIA: shared deploring without movement. Not WDYYB: no advice-seeking. Not Blemish: no sequential critique setting.

questions.prompt: What does the Blemish game provide Cass that direct comparison would not?
choices: Technical superiority that cannot be disputed because it is built on findings that are actually true, rather than on a claim that Cass is better than others
Recognition from the instructor
The ability to give more accurate critique than other students

explanation.gentle: Undisputable technical positioning is the specific payoff. A direct comparison could be challenged; accurate findings cannot. Instructor recognition is downstream. Accuracy describes the vehicle.
explanation.direct: Accuracy-grounded undisputable superiority is the payoff. Direct comparison can be disputed; accurate first-findings cannot. Instructor recognition is indirect.
explanation.competitive: The game's structural advantage over direct comparison: the findings are accurate so the positioning cannot be challenged.

questions.prompt: What do all three party game patterns share about the social stroke they pay?
choices: All three pay warmth-through-agreement or warmth-through-superiority strokes without requiring any player to be personally present with another specific person in the room
All three pay the same kind of stroke as marital games
All three pay negative strokes that players accept because positive strokes are unavailable

explanation.gentle: Warmth without personal presence is the shared feature. Marital game comparison misses the scale difference. Negative stroke framing misapplies Ch4.
explanation.direct: Agreement-warmth or superiority-warmth without personal disclosure is the shared payoff. Marital game equivalence is wrong on scale. Negative stroke framing misapplies the distinction.
explanation.competitive: Warmth without personal presence is the shared architecture. The three patterns differ in how they produce the warmth but all three produce it without genuine presence.

questions.prompt: How does the WDYYB pattern illustrate the ulterior transaction structure from Chapter 3?
choices: It is a complementary transaction because everyone is being agreeable
The social level of WDYYB is advice-seeking; the psychological level is a proof-of-insolubility operation. Both levels run simultaneously, and the ulterior level is the one that produces the payoff.
WDYYB is not an ulterior transaction because there is no hidden agenda

explanation.gentle: Two-level structure with ulterior payoff is the Ch3 connection. Advice-seeking is the social level; insolubility proof is the ulterior level. Calling it complementary misapplies Ch2. Denying the ulterior level refuses the structural analysis.
explanation.direct: Two-level transaction is the Ch3 connection. The ulterior level (insolubility proof) runs simultaneously with the social level (advice-seeking). Complementary misidentifies the transaction type. Denying the ulterior level refuses the analysis.
explanation.competitive: Ch3 connection: two levels simultaneously. Social level is advice-seeking; ulterior level is insolubility proof. Complementary is wrong. Denying the ulterior level is flat refusal of the structural analysis.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: The games in this chapter hide inside professional helping relationships. A supervisor and a supervisee, a coach and a student, a therapist and a client. The helper's job is to offer help, and the game uses the job as cover. Three patterns. I'm Only Trying To Help You: the helper offers help, the recipient accepts and does not use it, the help fails, and the helper has proof the recipient is hopeless while the helper is blameless. Wooden Leg: the recipient cites a real limitation as permanent exemption, and the helper accepts it because the limitation is real. Greenhouse: the client becomes a sophisticated user of the helper's vocabulary and uses it to describe patterns while not changing them. All three need both people to run, and the helper is not innocent of the structure. That is the chapter's defining claim.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Professional games run inside helping relationships where the helper's role provides the cover. Three patterns. I'm Only Trying To Help You: helper offers help, recipient predictably fails to use it, helper is proved blameless and recipient hopeless. Wooden Leg: recipient uses a real limitation as permanent exemption from accountability. Greenhouse: recipient uses sophisticated vocabulary to describe patterns rather than change them. All three require helper complicity, which is the chapter's distinguishing feature: the helper is structurally part of the game, not a bystander.

This distinguishes the professional game category from every other game in the catalog. In life games, marital games, and party games, the second player may be genuinely unaware they are participating in someone else's pattern. In professional games, the helper's role is the structure the game runs inside, and the helper's strokes are part of what the game is delivering. The diagnosis has to include the helper's side of the arrangement, which is the move professional training often does not teach.

This is the only chapter where diagnosing the game requires looking at both seats at the table.

The game is not between the client and some external antagonist. The game runs inside the helping relationship, with the helper as a structural participant. ITHY works because the helper needs to be helpful and the client needs to be failed. Wooden Leg works because the helper accepts the limitation as complete because disputing it would feel cruel. chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The games in this chapter are different from everything in the catalog so far because the helper is built into them. In life games, party games, and even marital games, the other person caught in the pattern is sometimes a player and sometimes a bystander who got pulled in. In professional games, the helper is there by profession, and the profession is what the game runs inside.

Ife's supervision with Rémy is the clearest example. Every Thursday for three years, Rémy has presented a case and Ife has offered perspective. Nothing in Rémy's practice has changed. The hour is about the arrangement: Ife gets the satisfaction of helping, Rémy gets professional attention.

Bo's Monday mornings with Caleb have a harder edge because Caleb's learning disability is real and well-documented. The disability is not the game. The deployment is. For two years, the disability has been Caleb's explanation for why he has not made progress on his degree, and for two years, Bo has accepted the explanation without asking whether Caleb has tried the accommodations that exist for his specific condition. The antithesis is the question that holds both realities at once: 'The disability is real. The accommodation is real. Which one do you want to try first?' That sentence refuses to let the limitation stand as the whole explanation without denying that the limitation is real.

Tamsin's therapy with Zara is the hardest of the three to see from inside the room. Zara is smart and well-read. Every session produces a new self-observation that is accurate and interesting. Tamsin has been rewarded by the sophistication of these conversations in a way she has not quite examined. The Greenhouse game, Berne's name for this pattern, runs on exactly that reward: the theory talk is the thing being delivered, not the thing being prepared for. The antithesis is Tamsin declining the reward and asking about experience instead of insight.

The chapter's central structural claim is the one that distinguishes it from every other catalog chapter. The helper is part of the game. The professional role is the cover. This means the diagnosis cannot come from looking only at the client. It has to come from the helper being willing to ask what they have been getting from the arrangement, and that question is not one professional training typically teaches.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne's consulting-room games category covers patterns that run inside helping relationships, and the distinguishing structural feature is that the helper is part of the game rather than a bystander. The helper's professional role is the cover that makes the game invisible from inside.

I'm Only Trying To Help You runs on a dual arrangement: the recipient accepts help and predictably fails to use it; the helper is left with proof that they tried and the recipient is hopeless. The helper's position ends up as I'm OK, you're not OK, and I did what I could. The antithesis requires the helper to ask what has actually changed in the recipient's situation over the course of the helping relationship, a question that breaks the generator contract of the helper role.

Wooden Leg runs on a real or claimed limitation deployed as a permanent exemption. The limitation is genuine; the game is in the deployment. The helper accepts the explanation because the limitation is real, which is precisely what the game requires. The antithesis holds both realities: the limitation is real and the agency is real, and the question is what the client wants to do with the available accommodations.

Greenhouse runs on sophisticated theory talk that substitutes for experience. The client uses the helping profession's vocabulary to observe and label their patterns with real insight, but the observations do not lead to different experiences. The helper is rewarded by the sophistication of the conversations and loses track of the goal. The antithesis is the helper's willingness to ask about concrete experience rather than additional insight.

The chapter's structural claim: the helper is part of the game. Diagnosing requires examining both sides. This is harder than it sounds because professional training focuses on the client's patterns, not on the helper's investment in how the work feels.

The three patterns — ITHY, Wooden Leg, Greenhouse — each run inside a legitimate professional structure. The legitimacy is what the game uses as cover, and the cover is what makes professional training poorly positioned to teach the diagnosis.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
Professional games are the most durable in the catalog because the helper's role provides the cover, and the cover is supported by the entire institutional structure of the helping profession. Supervisors are supposed to supervise. Coaches are supposed to coach. Therapists are supposed to work with insight. The games use those obligations.

I'm Only Trying To Help You runs on a mutual investment that neither party has named. The helper gets the satisfaction of being helpful. The recipient gets the structured attention of a professional who is required to engage with them. The help itself is the thing neither party actually needs, which is why nothing changes over years of meetings. The antithesis is the question the helper has not asked: what has actually changed in your situation since we started? That question breaks the generator contract and requires the helper to give up the strokes of being the reliable source of help.

Wooden Leg is the game that requires the most subtle handling because the limitation is real. The deployment of a real disability as a permanent exemption from agency is not a moral failure on the client's part; it is what has worked, and the helper has been rewarding the deployment by accepting it without question. The antithesis holds two realities at once: the limitation is real, and the accommodation exists to work with the limitation, not to replace the attempt.

Greenhouse is the game Berne saw most clearly in his own profession, and it runs on a specific reward structure: the helper is rewarded by the sophistication of the client's self-observations. The more articulate the client's pattern recognition, the more the helper feels the work is productive. The trap is that the pattern recognition is not the work; the work was supposed to produce different experiences. The antithesis is the helper's willingness to notice the reward and ask about experience.

The chapter's hardest claim is the one that turns the catalog into a tool for the helpers: the helper is part of the game. The role is the cover. Diagnosing the game requires examining what the helper has been getting from the arrangement, which is a question professional training often does not teach because the question cannot be answered from inside the role.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
The games in this chapter are the most durable in the catalog, and the reason is structural. In the previous catalog chapters, the other person in the game was sometimes a player and sometimes a bystander who had been pulled into someone else's pattern. In this chapter, the other person is always a helper whose job is to offer help, and the game runs inside the job. The professional role is the camouflage.

Berne observed these most clearly in his own profession, which is why the catalog calls them therapy-room games, but the structures show up in every helping relationship: clinical supervision, teaching, coaching, management mentoring, academic advising. Three patterns carry the chapter.

I'm Only Trying To Help You is the clearest. Ife and Rémy have been meeting for three years. Every week, Rémy presents a case. Every week, Ife offers perspective. Rémy is grateful. Rémy is also, by every external measure, an effective clinician whose practice has not materially changed since the meetings began. The game is not about the cases. The game is about the arrangement: Ife gets the satisfaction of being a helpful supervisor, Rémy gets a reliable structured hour of professional attention from someone who understands his work. Both are real payoffs. Neither party has named them. The antithesis is the question Ife has not asked in three years, and the reason she has not asked it is the same reason Rémy has kept coming: the arrangement is valuable to both of them for reasons that have nothing to do with the cases.

Wooden Leg is the hardest of the three to write about carefully because it involves real limitations. Caleb has a documented learning disability. The disability is real. Bo has been accepting the disability as the explanation for Caleb's lack of progress for two years. What Bo has not been doing is holding the reality of the disability alongside the reality of Caleb's agency. Accommodations exist; Caleb has not tried them; Bo has not asked why. The antithesis refuses the false choice: the disability is real, the accommodation is real, and the question is which one Caleb wants to try first.

Greenhouse is the pattern Berne watched most carefully in his own consulting room. Zara reads attachment theory and can describe her own relational patterns with real precision. Every session produces a new self-observation. Tamsin has been rewarded for the sophistication of these conversations in a way she has not examined. The sessions have become about the observations rather than about what the observations were supposed to prepare Zara for, which is different experiences in her actual life. The antithesis is Tamsin noticing, out loud, that the sessions have become the theory talk, and asking about experience instead.

The hardest structural claim in the chapter is the one that turns the whole catalog into a tool for the helpers as well as for the helped. The helper is part of the game. The professional role is the cover. This means the chapter cannot be read only as an instruction for clients to recognize when their therapist or supervisor or coach is playing along with their pattern. It has to be read, and harder, as an instruction for professionals to ask what they have been getting from their most long-running helping relationships. That is a question professional training often does not teach, because the honest answer sometimes undermines the arrangement that funds the training in the first place.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
Berne's category of consulting-room games has a structural feature that distinguishes it from every other catalog category: the second player is a helping professional whose role is built into the game's architecture. The helper is not a bystander who got caught in the client's pattern; the helper is there by job description, and the job description is what the game runs inside.

I'm Only Trying To Help You operates on a mutual investment that neither party has named. Ife supervises Rémy every Thursday for three years. Rémy presents cases. Ife offers perspective. Both are good at their work. Neither has asked what has materially changed in Rémy's practice over that span, because the answer would require both of them to give up something that is not in the formal frame of the supervision. Ife would give up the reliable satisfaction of being a helpful supervisor. Rémy would give up the structured hour of professional attention from someone who understands the work. Both payoffs are real. The antithesis is the question that names them, and the question is not in the formal job description of either participant.

Wooden Leg operates on the structural honesty of a real limitation. The client has a real disability, a real loss, a real developmental difference, and the game is in how the real thing is deployed. Bo has been treating Caleb's documented learning disability as the total explanation for two years because the alternative has felt like denial. The antithesis holds both realities: the limitation is real, and the available accommodations are real, and the question is which accommodation the client wants to try. The antithesis is structurally simple and emotionally difficult because it refuses the comfort of treating the limitation as either the whole story or a story to be disputed.

Greenhouse operates on the sophistication-reward feedback loop in any helping relationship where the helper's profession has a developed vocabulary. The client learns the vocabulary and uses it with real insight; the helper is rewarded by the sophistication of the conversations; the conversations become the work rather than the preparation for the work. The antithesis is the helper's willingness to notice the reward structure and to ask about experience instead of insight.

The chapter's hardest structural claim is the diagnostic one. The helper is part of the game. Diagnosing the game by looking only at the client misses the point. The helper has to be willing to ask what they have been getting from the arrangement, which is a question professional training typically does not teach, because asking it honestly sometimes reveals that the arrangement is not about the work it claims to be about.

The three patterns divide the work cleanly. ITHY uses the satisfaction of helping as the reward. Wooden Leg uses the reality of a limitation as the cover for accountability. Greenhouse uses the sophistication of insight as a substitute for change. Each is a different arrangement; each requires the helper to examine their side of it. The chapter's honest difficulty is that the examination is rarely taught and the question that triggers it is rarely comfortable.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The games that run inside professional helping relationships are the most durable games in the catalog, and the reason is not subtle. The helper has an obligation to engage. The professional frame provides cover. The institution pays for the arrangement. The game is invisible from inside the role because the role is doing exactly what it is supposed to do, one session at a time, year after year, while nothing changes.

I'm Only Trying To Help You runs on the mutual benefit of a continuing arrangement neither party has reason to examine. Ife gets the satisfaction of supervising Rémy. Rémy gets the structured attention of a senior clinician who understands his work. Both are real professional goods. Neither of them requires the cases to actually change for the goods to be delivered. The meetings have become the service, and the service is about the relationship, not the cases. This is not failure on either side. It is the game succeeding at being a game, and the antithesis requires one of them to give up the goods in order to find out whether the relationship was ever about the work.

Wooden Leg is the game that most tests whether the reader can hold complexity. The limitation is real. The accommodation is real. The client has not tried the accommodation. The helper has not asked why. Each of those facts is true, and none of them individually constitute the game. The game is the structure in which the limitation stands as the total explanation without ever being put alongside the accommodations. The antithesis is Bo saying, in one sentence, both true things: the disability is real, and the college has a specific accommodation for this disability, and the question is which one to try first. That sentence is uncomfortable for both parties because it breaks the structural honesty that has been holding the arrangement together, and it has to be held by the helper because the client cannot be expected to break it from inside the deployment.

Greenhouse is the pattern Berne named in his own profession and the one that most directly exposes the reward structure of helping work. The client becomes a sophisticated user of the helper's own vocabulary. The helper is rewarded by the sophistication. The sessions produce observations that feel like progress. They are not progress. They are beautifully articulated descriptions of unchanged experiences. The antithesis is the helper's willingness to notice that they have been rewarded by the sophistication and to ask, in the next session, whether the conversation Zara planned with her sister last week actually happened. That question declines the reward of the interesting session in exchange for information about the experience the session was supposed to prepare her for.

The hardest thing in the chapter is the claim that turns the catalog on the helpers. The helper is part of the game. The role is the cover. Diagnosing the game requires asking what the helper has been getting from the arrangement, and the answer is often something that professional training would rather not name because naming it threatens the institutional structures that employ the professional in the first place.

activationPrompt.gentle: Think of a helping relationship you are part of, as helper or recipient. Has anything objectively changed over its course? If not, what is each of you getting from the arrangement that has kept it running?
activationPrompt.direct: Name the longest-running helping relationship in your life. Identify what has actually changed over its duration. Name what each party has been getting from the arrangement independent of the stated work.
activationPrompt.competitive: Name the helping relationship in your life that has produced the least visible change relative to the time invested. Identify the reward each party is receiving. If the rewards are more stable than the work, the game is running.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: Can you identify a moment in a helping relationship when you noticed you were getting something from the arrangement that was not the stated work? What was it?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Name a helping relationship where the stated work has not progressed. Identify specifically what you have been rewarded by in the arrangement. The reward is the game's payment to you.
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Name the helping relationship where you (as helper or recipient) have been most invested in the continuation of the arrangement itself, separate from the work. State what you have been getting. That is the game's payment.

selfCheckPrompts.gentle: If you were to ask, in your most long-running helping relationship, 'what has actually changed since we started?', what do you predict would happen?
selfCheckPrompts.direct: Predict the outcome of asking, in your longest-running helping relationship, what has objectively changed since it began. What would you expect from the other party, and what would you expect from yourself in response?
selfCheckPrompts.competitive: Run the experiment in your head: the question asked in the next session of your longest helping relationship. What has changed? Would the question end the arrangement, transform it, or be absorbed? Your answer tells you what the arrangement has been for.

predictionPrompt.gentle: If the helpers in the three examples (Ife, Bo, and Tamsin) each asked the diagnostic question of their clients in the next session, what do you predict would happen in each case?
predictionPrompt.direct: Predict, for each of the three anchor examples, what would happen if the helper asked the antithesis question in the next session. Which relationships would end, which would transform, and which would be absorbed back into the same pattern?
predictionPrompt.competitive: Run the three experiments: Ife asks Rémy what has changed; Bo asks Caleb which accommodation to try; Tamsin asks Zara whether the sister conversation happened. Which helper-client pair survives the antithesis, and which does not? The survival depends on whether the relationship was ever about the work.

scenario.gentle: Ife is in the small supervision room on the third floor of the community mental health center at 2pm on Thursday. Rémy has just finished presenting a case. It is the third year of these weekly meetings. The case Rémy presented is structurally similar to the one he presented two weeks ago. Ife offered a perspective she has offered in various forms across the three years. Rémy took a note. The hour ends. Ife walks back to her office and notices, clearly for the first time, that nothing about Rémy's practice has materially changed in three years of supervision.
scenario.direct: Thursday supervision room, 2pm. Rémy (case presentation, similar structure to recent weeks): the client with substance use history and complicated relationship with adult daughter. Ife (offering perspective): holding the client's agency and the daughter's separateness in the same frame. Rémy takes a note. Three years of this. Rémy is an effective clinician. His practice has not materially changed across the three years.
scenario.competitive: Three years of Thursday supervision. Rémy is good at his job. Ife is good at hers. The cases being presented are structurally identical week over week. Nothing about Rémy's practice has changed. Ife is sitting in her office after the meeting and asking herself, for the first time, what the three years have been for.

whatToDo.gentle: The question Ife can bring to the next meeting is not a direct confrontation. It is a genuine inquiry: 'Rémy, I want to step back with you for a minute. Looking at the last three years, what do you think has actually changed in how you work? I am asking because I am not sure I can name something specific.' The question treats Rémy as the expert on his own practice and opens the door without slamming it.
whatToDo.direct: Bring the diagnostic question to the next supervision: 'What has actually changed in how you work over the last three years of our meetings?' The question is not accusatory. It is a genuine inquiry that requires both of you to step outside the weekly case-presentation frame.
whatToDo.competitive: Ask the question: 'In three years, what has changed in your practice?' If Rémy answers honestly and names something, the supervision is not a game, or was but is not anymore. If Rémy names nothing, both of you have information you did not have before the question.

whyItMatters.gentle: Supervision relationships that run for years without producing visible change have become something other than supervision. The question about what has changed is the only way to find out whether the relationship can still do the work it was created to do.
whyItMatters.direct: Long-running supervision without visible progress is a reliable signal that the arrangement has drifted from its stated purpose. The diagnostic question is the minimum intervention required to find out whether it can be recovered.
whyItMatters.competitive: Three years is a long time to be paying an institution for a supervision arrangement that is not moving. The diagnostic question is the cheapest possible first move, and it respects both parties by refusing to continue the arrangement on autopilot.

scenario.gentle: Tamsin is in the fourth session of the third month of therapy with Zara. Zara is describing a pattern she has just noticed in herself, and the description is precise and psychologically sophisticated. Tamsin is noticing that she is being drawn into the sophistication of the conversation, and she is also remembering that Zara said last week she was going to have a specific conversation with her sister before this session.
scenario.direct: TAMSIN: I want to pause on what you just said. Before you expand on the pattern, I want to ask about last week. You said you were going to talk to your sister. Did that conversation happen? ZARA: (pause) No, not yet. I was going to, but I wanted to think about it more first. TAMSIN: I notice we have been talking about the pattern and we have not talked about the conversation. Can we stay with the conversation for a few minutes?
scenario.competitive: Zara is describing a new self-observation, accurate and interesting. Tamsin is catching herself being rewarded by the sophistication of the description and is asking herself whether she has noticed, in three months of sessions, that the conversations have become about insights rather than about experience. She is deciding whether to name this or to continue the session in its current shape.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask the experience question gently but directly. 'Before we expand on the observation, I want to ask about the specific conversation you mentioned last week. Did it happen?' If it did not, that is the thing to sit with, not the new insight. If it did, ask what happened in it, not what Zara thought about it afterward.
whatToDo.direct: Interrupt the insight and ask about experience. 'Did the conversation with your sister happen?' If no, sit with that. If yes, ask what happened, not what Zara concluded. The experience is the unit; the insight is the description.
whatToDo.competitive: Name the pattern in one sentence without weaponizing it: 'I notice I have been finding our pattern-spotting sessions very engaging, and I want to balance them by asking about concrete experiences between sessions. What actually happened since we last met?' That sentence declines the reward of the interesting session without shaming Zara.

whyItMatters.gentle: Therapy that becomes an ongoing conversation about insight is not the same as therapy that produces different experiences. The distinction is hard to see when the insights are genuinely good.
whyItMatters.direct: Insight-substitution in therapy is Berne's Greenhouse game at full form. The sessions feel productive because they are interesting. The experience the insights were supposed to prepare for is not happening. The antithesis is the helper declining the interesting conversation to ask about the experience.
whyItMatters.competitive: A therapy that produces better descriptions of unchanged experiences is not serving the client. The helper is rewarded by the sophistication; the client is rewarded by the attention; the stated work does not happen. Naming experience over insight is the antithesis and it is expensive for the helper because it declines the reward.

scenario.gentle: Bo has been meeting Caleb in the student success office every Monday at 10am for four semesters. Caleb's learning disability is real, documented, and not in dispute. Every meeting, Caleb describes his progress (minimal) and explains why the disability has made it difficult. Bo has been nodding and offering support. Today, Bo has printed a list of the accommodations available for Caleb's specific disability, none of which Caleb has tried, and is trying to find a way to bring the list into the conversation without making Caleb feel attacked.
scenario.direct: Monday, 10am, student success office. Bo (holding a list of available accommodations): Caleb, I have been thinking about our meetings over the last four semesters. I want to try something different today. I have a list of the accommodations our office offers for your specific disability. I am not saying your disability is not real. I am saying these accommodations exist. I want to ask which one you would be willing to try for two weeks. CALEB: (pause) I did not know there were this many.
scenario.competitive: Bo has been sitting with this list for three weeks before bringing it to the meeting. The decision was not whether to bring it but how to bring it without the conversation collapsing into a defensive argument about whether the disability is real. The disability is real. That is not in question. What is in question is whether anything else is also true at the same time.

whatToDo.gentle: Lead with the acknowledgment of reality before the list. 'Your disability is real and the documentation is clear. I want to hold that alongside something else: our office has these accommodations, and I want to ask which one you would be willing to try for two weeks. Not forever. Two weeks, as an experiment.' The sentence holds both realities and names the experiment as temporary, which reduces the cost of trying.
whatToDo.direct: Hold both truths in the same sentence: 'The disability is real and these accommodations exist. Which one would you try for two weeks?' Then wait. The wait is uncomfortable and necessary. Caleb's response is information about whether the game is still running or whether this is the moment it ends.
whatToDo.competitive: Bring both facts and the two-week frame in one move: 'The disability is real. These accommodations exist for it. Pick one to try for two weeks.' The brevity is the point. Long versions give the game more room to run. Short versions force the choice.

whyItMatters.gentle: Accommodations for real disabilities exist specifically so the limitation is not the whole story. Holding both the limitation and the accommodation as real is the only way to honor the student while refusing to let the game continue.
whyItMatters.direct: Wooden Leg runs on treating the real limitation as the total explanation. The accommodation's existence disrupts the totality without denying the limitation. Holding both is the mechanical antithesis.
whyItMatters.competitive: A student success office that never brings up accommodations because the disability is real has stopped being a success office. The accommodations exist specifically because real limitations are not the whole story, and bringing them into the conversation is the office's actual function.

scenario.gentle: I am the senior supervisor at the training clinic, and I am meeting with Obi, who started supervising interns this semester. He is telling me that one of his interns, Jade, keeps presenting the same kind of case every week, and that he has been offering the same kind of perspective, and that he is starting to feel like something is off but he is not sure what. I recognize the shape of what he is describing before he finishes describing it.
scenario.direct: First-person: I am Inara, the senior supervisor. Obi is new to supervising and is describing to me what sounds like the early shape of an I'm Only Trying To Help You pattern with his intern Jade. He is smart and has caught that something is off. He does not yet have a name for it. I want to give him the diagnostic without handing him a label that might feel like it resolves the issue.
scenario.competitive: Obi is describing a three-month-old supervision pattern and asking me what is happening. I can see the game clearly. I can also see that if I hand him the word 'game' too quickly, he will either feel accused of failing Jade or will start using the word as a weapon. I want to give him the diagnostic without giving him the vocabulary yet.

whatToDo.gentle: Ask Obi a question instead of naming the pattern: 'When you leave those supervision sessions, how do you feel? And when you think about what Jade will take into her practice from the session, what do you actually expect?' Those questions give Obi the diagnostic without labeling anything.
whatToDo.direct: Ask two diagnostic questions: 'How do you feel after these sessions?' and 'What do you expect Jade to do differently next week?' The first surfaces Obi's investment in the arrangement; the second surfaces whether the sessions have a theory of change. Both together map the game without naming it.
whatToDo.competitive: Two questions, in sequence, with time to answer each: 'How do you feel after these sessions?' and 'What do you actually expect to be different in Jade's practice next week?' The first reveals his reward; the second reveals the missing theory of change. Name nothing yet. Let Obi bring the diagnosis to himself.

whyItMatters.gentle: Senior supervisors who hand new supervisors the vocabulary of games without the diagnostic questions produce new supervisors who label their interns. The diagnostic questions are the slower, more useful tool.
whyItMatters.direct: Teaching new supervisors to diagnose patterns without weaponizing the vocabulary is the slower, better training approach. Questions about what the helper is feeling and expecting carry the diagnostic without the labels that make the game feel like a judgment of the client.
whyItMatters.competitive: A training clinic where new supervisors are given the game vocabulary without the questions that make it a diagnostic tool produces a generation of supervisors who see games everywhere and lose the ability to be useful to the clients who need them. The questions are the training; the labels are the shortcut that undermines the training.

scenario.gentle: Tova is walking home from her weekly session with the life coach she has been working with for a year. She is thinking about the session she just had, which was warm and productive and left her feeling like she understood herself better. She is also thinking about the fact that she has been feeling that way after every session for a year, and that the things she was supposed to be working on at the start of the year are the things she is still supposed to be working on. She does not yet have a word for what is bothering her.
scenario.direct: Inner monologue, walking home. Tova: I feel good after every session. Every session produces an insight I find genuinely helpful. The goals we set at the start of the year are the same goals we reset last week in slightly different words. The sessions are productive. My life is not different. I am trying to hold those two things together and I am not sure what they add up to.
scenario.competitive: Tova is walking the six blocks home from her coach's office and the session was good, the way every session for a year has been good, and she is looking at the year in aggregate for the first time and the aggregate is zero. The sessions are real. The insights are real. Her life is not different. She is doing the math and the math does not match the stated purpose of the coaching, and she does not yet know what to do with the mismatch.

whatToDo.gentle: Tova can bring this to the next session without framing it as an accusation: 'I have been thinking about the year. I have appreciated these sessions, and I am also noticing that the goals we set last January are the same goals we are still working on. I want to ask you what you think about that.' The question gives the coach a chance to engage with the pattern rather than defend against it.
whatToDo.direct: Name the pattern at the start of the next session. 'I want to pause on something. The goals from January are the same goals. I want to ask what you think about that before we continue.' The question invites the coach into the diagnostic rather than accusing them of failing.
whatToDo.competitive: Open the next session with the question: 'The goals from January are the same goals today. I want to talk about what that means before we do anything else.' The coach's response is information. A coach who engages with the question is not running the game, or was but is willing to stop. A coach who deflects is running it and does not want it named.

whyItMatters.gentle: Clients who notice the aggregate pattern of a helping relationship are in the best position to diagnose it, because they can feel the mismatch in their own lives. Bringing the observation into the session is the move that either recovers the relationship or reveals that it cannot be recovered.
whyItMatters.direct: The client-side diagnostic is often the most honest diagnostic available because the client has direct access to whether their life is different. Bringing the observation into the session is the cheapest possible intervention.
whyItMatters.competitive: A year of coaching that has not changed the things the coaching was supposed to change is a year of stroke delivery that has been funded as coaching. The client naming the mismatch is the only intervention that has a chance of recovering the arrangement, and it is cheaper to make now than it will be in year two.

examples.title: Xavier notices what he is getting

scenario.gentle: Xavier has been in a mentoring relationship with a former professor, Nils-Erik, for seven years. They meet quarterly for coffee. Nils-Erik offers career advice. Xavier takes notes. The quarterly meetings have been a stable anchor in Xavier's professional life. Looking back at seven years of them, Xavier is noticing that the career moves he has made have been the ones he would have made without the advice, and that what he has actually been getting from the meetings is the experience of being taken seriously by someone whose seriousness mattered to him.
scenario.direct: Narrative flashback across seven years. Xavier reviews the mentoring arc: twenty-eight meetings, career advice received, career moves made. The career moves and the advice do not have a causal relationship; he would have made the same moves. What he has been getting is the weight of Nils-Erik's attention on his career, which matters to him independently of the advice. He is now looking at this clearly and asking what the relationship has actually been.
scenario.competitive: Seven years, twenty-eight meetings. Xavier is doing the accounting. The career advice has been kind and mostly generic. The career decisions have been his own. The thing he has been actually getting from Nils-Erik is the validation of being taken seriously by a person whose seriousness is scarce and valuable. The mentorship has been about the validation all along, and neither of them named it because the mentorship vocabulary was easier.

whatToDo.gentle: Xavier does not have to end the relationship to see it clearly. He can, at the next coffee, mention what he has actually valued: 'Looking at the seven years, I want you to know that what I have valued most has been the weight of your attention on my career, more than any specific advice. That is a real thing and I am grateful for it.' Naming it converts the arrangement from a mentorship that was not quite working into a friendship that might work better.
whatToDo.direct: Name what you have actually valued. 'What I have gotten most from these meetings is the seriousness of your attention on my work, more than the advice itself. I want to say that out loud.' The sentence converts the arrangement from one thing into another more honest thing, and the relationship can continue on the new basis if both want it to.
whatToDo.competitive: Say it at the next meeting. 'Seven years in, what I have valued is your attention, not the advice. I want to be honest about that.' The sentence ends the mentorship-shaped relationship and opens the door to whatever honest relationship exists between you. If Nils-Erik meets the honesty, the new relationship is better than the old one. If he does not, you have information you did not have.

whyItMatters.gentle: Some helping relationships are actually friendships that have been running inside the helping frame because the helping frame is what the two people had access to. Naming what the relationship has actually been is not an ending; it is often the beginning of the relationship as it really was.
whyItMatters.direct: Mentor relationships that have become de facto friendships benefit from the honest naming of what they actually are. The mentoring vocabulary can be a cover for real affection that has no other socially available frame.
whyItMatters.competitive: Seven years of generic career advice between people who actually like each other is seven years of the helping frame standing in for the actual relationship. Naming the actual relationship is the only way to let it be what it has been all along.

questions.prompt: What structurally distinguishes professional and therapy-room games from the other games in the catalog?
choices: They involve more serious psychological issues
The helper is structurally part of the game by profession; the professional role is the game's cover, and the game cannot run without the helper's investment in the arrangement
They only occur in clinical settings

explanation.gentle: The helper's role as structural cover is the defining feature. The chapter is explicit that the helper is not a bystander. Serious psychological issues is not the structural definition. Clinical settings is wrong: the patterns show up in supervision, coaching, teaching, academic advising, and management mentoring.
explanation.direct: Helper-as-structural-part is the definition. Severity is not the category criterion. Clinical settings is an empirical overstatement; the chapter names supervision, coaching, teaching, advising, and mentoring as the relevant settings.
explanation.competitive: The helper is the cover. That is the structural claim. Severity misidentifies the category. Clinical-setting framing understates where the games run.

questions.prompt: In the three-year supervision arrangement between Ife and Rémy, what are both parties getting from the arrangement that has kept it running?
choices: Nothing; the arrangement is simply going through the motions
Professional credit and continuing education credits

Ife gets the satisfaction of being a helpful supervisor; Rémy gets the structured hour of professional attention from someone who understands his work. Both are real goods. Neither requires the cases to actually change.

explanation.gentle: Both real goods are the answer. The chapter is explicit that the arrangement is not nothing; it is valuable to both parties for reasons that have nothing to do with the cases. Credit-hours framing is a surface explanation that misses the psychological-level payoff.
explanation.direct: Mutual goods that do not require the cases to change is the chapter's claim. 'Nothing' misses the real payoffs. Credit-hour framing is the social level; the game is at the psychological level.
explanation.competitive: Two real goods. 'Nothing' denies the game's payments. Credit hours describes the social frame; the game runs at the level the credit hours do not see.

questions.prompt: Bo is working with Caleb, who has a real documented learning disability. What is the antithesis to the Wooden Leg pattern Bo has been accepting?
choices: Hold the reality of the disability alongside the reality of the available accommodations in the same sentence, and ask which accommodation Caleb wants to try
Tell Caleb the disability is not as limiting as he thinks
Refuse to meet with Caleb until he has tried an accommodation

explanation.gentle: Hold both realities is the antithesis. Denying the limitation falls into the trap the chapter is specifically trying to avoid. Refusing to meet is punitive and abandons the helping role entirely.
explanation.direct: Both-realities-in-one-sentence is the mechanical antithesis. Denial of the limitation replaces one error with another. Refusal to meet is abandonment, not antithesis.
explanation.competitive: Hold both facts together. Denial is the error the chapter explicitly warns against. Refusal to meet exits the helping relationship, which is not an antithesis.

questions.prompt: In the Greenhouse pattern between Tamsin and Zara, what has Tamsin been rewarded by that has made the game invisible from inside the helping role?
choices: The length of the therapy relationship
The fees she is being paid
The sophistication of Zara's self-observations, which has made the sessions feel productive even though Zara's life has not changed

explanation.gentle: Reward by sophistication is the chapter's specific claim about Greenhouse. Length and fees are surface structural features that do not explain the game's durability from the helper's side.
explanation.direct: Sophistication-reward feedback loop is the mechanism. Length and fees are not the psychological-level payment to the helper.
explanation.competitive: Sophistication reward. Length is correlation not mechanism. Fees are the social-level frame of the relationship, not the psychological-level game payment.

questions.prompt: A new teacher keeps meeting with a veteran teacher for weekly mentoring. Every week the new teacher brings a classroom management problem; every week the veteran offers advice; the new teacher takes notes and thanks the veteran. Nothing in the new teacher's classroom has changed in six months. What pattern does this resemble?
choices: Wooden Leg
I'm Only Trying To Help You
Greenhouse

explanation.gentle: ITHY pattern. Help offered, accepted, not used, helper's role preserved, recipient's classroom unchanged. Wooden Leg would require the new teacher citing a limitation as the reason. Greenhouse would require sophisticated pattern-recognition language.
explanation.direct: ITHY: help offered and not used, with the helper blameless. Wooden Leg needs a real limitation deployed as exemption. Greenhouse needs vocabulary substituting for experience.
explanation.competitive: ITHY by structure. Wooden Leg needs the limitation framing; Greenhouse needs the vocabulary substitution. Neither of those is present here.

questions.prompt: According to the chapter, why is the helper structurally part of the game rather than an accidental participant?
choices: Because the helper's professional role requires them to offer help, and the game runs inside that professional obligation, which is what makes the game invisible from inside the role
Because helpers secretly want their clients to fail
Because helpers are not adequately trained

explanation.gentle: The professional role as structural cover is the chapter's claim. The helper is not malicious (secretly wanting failure is a moral accusation the chapter refuses) and not inadequately trained (the claim is that training typically does not teach the diagnostic, not that training is bad). The role itself is the cover.
explanation.direct: Professional role as structural cover is the mechanism. Malice-framing is the moral accusation the chapter refuses. Inadequate-training framing misreads the chapter's claim about what training typically does not teach.
explanation.competitive: The role is the cover. Malice framing moralizes the helper. Training-inadequacy framing is a different claim than the one the chapter makes.

questions.prompt: A manager has been giving weekly one-on-ones to a direct report for a year. The direct report presents the same kind of interpersonal problem each week. The manager offers perspective. The direct report is grateful but unchanged. Which game pattern is this most consistent with?
choices: Greenhouse, because the report keeps articulating their situation
Wooden Leg, because the report has a workplace difficulty
I'm Only Trying To Help You, because the manager keeps offering help that is received but not used

explanation.gentle: ITHY is the match. The report accepts help and does not use it; the manager is positioned as having tried.
